meta.title: Wolfspeed — Robert Feurle's silicon carbide power semiconductors through the Mohawk Valley ramp, Chapter 11 restructuring, and the EV/AI/industrial demand cycle
meta.abstract: Wolfspeed, Inc. (NYSE: WOLF) is a Durham, North Carolina-headquartered pure-play silicon carbide (SiC) power semiconductor company that emerged from the multi-year transformation of Cree, Inc. through the LED divestiture (sold to SMART Global Holdings as CreeLED in 2021) and the Wolfspeed renaming (October 2021). The company designs and manufactures SiC bare wafers (150mm and 200mm), SiC epi wafers, and discrete SiC MOSFET and SiC Schottky diode devices serving electric vehicle traction inverters, AI data center power supplies, renewable energy inverters, industrial motor drives, and broader power-conversion applications. Strategic narrative through 2024-2026 centers on (a) the Mohawk Valley New York 200mm SiC fab ramp (first dedicated 200mm SiC fab globally; multi-billion-dollar capex deployed across 2022-2025), (b) the John W. Pope Saxapahaw North Carolina materials expansion, (c) the June 2025 Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing and restructuring framework (debt-for-equity exchange, reorganization plan emergence expected 2025-2026), (d) the strategic CEO transition from Gregg Lowe to Thomas Werner (interim) to Robert Feurle (appointed May 2025), and (e) the EV SiC traction inverter demand cycle volatility (Stellantis design-in, Mercedes-Benz wins, broader Tier-1 customer base) against the AI data center 800V HVDC SiC opportunity and the industrial/renewable end-market base.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
Wolfspeed, Inc. entered 2026 as a restructured pure-play silicon carbide power semiconductor company — leaner on debt, still heavy on execution risk, and operating the world's first dedicated 200-millimetre SiC fab at a moment when the electrification cycle it was built to serve had grown simultaneously more promising and more volatile. The Durham, North Carolina–headquartered company trades on the NYSE under the ticker WOLF and operates Mohawk Valley fab in Marcy, New York as its principal industrial asset.

## Heritage: From Cree to Pure-Play SiC

Wolfspeed traces its origins to Cree Research, founded in 1987 at North Carolina State University by Eric Hunter, F. Neal Hunter, and colleagues, commercialising compound semiconductor technology pioneered in the university's materials labs. The company went public on NASDAQ in 1993 and spent three decades as the dominant name in SiC and GaN-on-SiC technology, branching into blue LEDs and eventually lighting. That multi-product identity proved strategically limiting as the power semiconductor inflection approached.

Under chief executive Gregg Lowe — who took the role in 2017 — the company executed a two-step divestiture that stripped away everything not pure-play SiC power. In 2021, Cree sold its LED business to SMART Global Holdings as the CreeLED brand, and in October 2021 formally renamed the remaining entity Wolfspeed, Inc. to signal an explicit strategic identity. In December 2023, the RF semiconductor unit — legacy Cree/Wolfspeed RF — was divested to MACOM Technology Solutions for $125 million in cash plus $50 million in MACOM stock, completing the transformation. From December 2023 onward, Wolfspeed's entire commercial focus rested on silicon carbide power.

## Three Product Families

The restructured business runs three product families along the SiC value chain. SiC bare wafers — both mature 150mm and the emerging 200mm generation — serve both internal device fabrication and a merchant substrate supply business that counts Infineon, STMicroelectronics, onsemi, Bosch, and Rohm among its customers. SiC epitaxial wafers add a second layer of vertical integration. SiC discrete power devices — principally MOSFETs spanning 650 V through 3,300 V voltage classes and Schottky diodes — serve EV traction inverters, solar and wind inverters, industrial motor drives, rail traction, and, increasingly, AI data centre high-voltage power conversion.

## Financial Snapshot and the Mohawk Valley Ramp

Full-year fiscal 2025 revenue, for the year ended 29 June 2025, came in at [$757.6 million](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000895419/000089541925000110/wolf-20250629.htm), down from $807.2 million in fiscal 2024 as industrial and energy market softness more than offset automotive growth. The GAAP gross margin was negative 16 percent; the non-GAAP gross margin was 2 percent. Underutilisation charges at Mohawk Valley totalled $105.2 million for the full year, declining from $124.4 million in fiscal 2024 — evidence of incremental ramp progress, if not yet decisive yield economics.

The clearest sign of Mohawk Valley's forward trajectory was the fourth-quarter Mohawk Valley revenue figure: [$94.1 million](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000895419/000089541925000107/ex991q4-25.htm) in Q4 FY2025, up 130 percent from $41 million in the same quarter a year earlier. Wolfspeed disclosed in June 2024 that Mohawk Valley had reached [20 percent wafer-start utilisation](https://investor.wolfspeed.com/news/news-details/2024/Wolfspeed-Announces-Key-Milestones-and-Operational-Update/default.aspx); the company subsequently shifted to Mohawk Valley revenue as its primary ramp metric rather than disclosing utilisation percentages.

## Chapter 11 Filing and Emergence

With approximately $6.7 billion in funded debt and annual cash interest near $400 million, the capital structure had become unsustainable against a pre-profit revenue base. On 30 June 2025 — one day after fiscal year-end — Wolfspeed filed for Chapter 11 protection in the [U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of Texas](https://dm.epiq11.com/case/wolfspeed/info) (Case No. 25-90163), before Judge Christopher M. Lopez. The filing was prepackaged: a restructuring support agreement executed 22 June 2025 had already secured the support of approximately 97 percent of senior secured noteholders and approximately 67 percent of convertible noteholders.

The plan confirmed on 8 September 2025; Wolfspeed emerged from Chapter 11 on 29 September 2025 — a 91-day restructuring. Post-emergence funded debt stood at approximately $2.1 billion, a roughly 70 percent reduction; annual cash interest fell from approximately $400 million to approximately $160 million. Convertible noteholders received 56.3 percent of new equity; Renesas Electronics received 38.7 percent; existing equity holders received up to 5 percent as a creditor gift. The plan established an enterprise value of $2.35–$2.85 billion at emergence.

## CHIPS Act, 48D Tax Credits, and EV Design Wins

The Biden administration announced a [preliminary memorandum of terms for $750 million](https://www.commerce.gov/news/press-releases/2024/10/biden-harris-administration-announces-preliminary-terms-wolfspeed) in proposed direct CHIPS Act funding in October 2024, earmarked for Mohawk Valley and the John W. Pope Manufacturing Center in Siler City, North Carolina. That PMT never converted to a final award. In its place, the Section 48D Advanced Manufacturing Investment Credit route provided material liquidity: Wolfspeed received [$698.6 million in IRS cash tax refunds](https://investor.wolfspeed.com/news/news-details/2025/Wolfspeed-Receives-698-6-Million-in-Section-48D-Cash-Tax-Refunds-from-IRS/default.aspx) in December 2025, boosting the post-emergence cash balance to approximately $1.5 billion and enabling the retirement of roughly $175 million in debt.

On the demand side, fiscal 2025 design wins were described in the annual report as "second highest in company history," and the number of vehicle models incorporating Wolfspeed SiC grew approximately four-fold between 2023 and 2024. A January 2023 [long-term supply agreement with Mercedes-Benz](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20230104005311/en/Wolfspeed-Silicon-Carbide-Devices-Power-Future-Mercedes-Benz-Electric-Vehicle-Platforms) for multiple EV platforms, drawing on both the Durham legacy fab and Mohawk Valley, remains the marquee named automotive relationship. Wolfspeed's Generation 4 SiC technology, commercially launched in January 2025, claims up to 80 percent less switching loss versus silicon and approximately 10 percent EV range improvement.

## Feurle, and the Questions Ahead

Robert Feurle, 54, assumed the role of president and chief executive on 1 May 2025, midway through the restructuring. He brings a compound semiconductor and memory background spanning Siemens, Infineon — where he had previously worked on Infineon's 2016 proposed acquisition of Wolfspeed from Cree — Qimonda, Micron, and ams-OSRAM, where he ran the opto-semiconductors business unit managing more than 10,000 employees globally.

The dossier's central questions: whether Mohawk Valley's utilisation trajectory translates into positive gross margins within a credible planning horizon; whether the EV design-win pipeline converts into volume shipment revenue at Stellantis, Mercedes-Benz, and the broader Tier-1 base; whether the 800V HVDC data-centre power opportunity matures fast enough to diversify away from automotive cycle risk; whether CHIPS Act direct funding materialises under the current administration; and whether the post-emergence capital structure — $2.1 billion of debt against a sub-$800 million revenue base — is durable enough to fund the ramp to profitability against Infineon, STMicroelectronics, onsemi, and Rohm.

chapters.title: From 1987 Cree founding through LED/RF divestitures to Wolfspeed pure-play and Chapter 11
chapters.body:
## Roots in the Research Triangle, 1987–1993

The company that would eventually file for Chapter 11 protection in June 2025 began with a materials insight rather than a market plan. In 1987, a small group of researchers affiliated with North Carolina State University — among them Neal Hunter and Eric Hunter — established Cree Research, named for the crystal-growth technique at the heart of their work: chemical vapor deposition of silicon carbide. SiC had long fascinated materials scientists for its extraordinary thermal conductivity, breakdown field, and electron-saturation velocity, properties that made it theoretically superior to silicon for high-voltage and high-frequency applications. What Cree's founders recognised was that turning that theoretical superiority into manufacturable devices required solving a fundamental substrate problem: SiC crystals of commercial quality did not yet exist at scale, and the defect densities that plagued early boules made device yields impractical. Cree set out to fix that.

The early years were spent grinding through the materials science. The team mastered seeded sublimation growth — a technique for producing single-crystal SiC boules — and began producing the world's first commercially viable SiC wafers. That substrate expertise gave Cree an entry into blue and green light-emitting diodes, a product area that would come to define the company for two decades before it became an obstacle. In 1989, Cree shipped the first commercial blue LED built on a SiC substrate. The device was dim by later standards, but it demonstrated that wide-bandgap compound semiconductors could be manufactured and sold, not merely theorised about.

In February 1993, Cree Research completed an initial public offering on NASDAQ, raising capital that allowed it to extend both its materials platform and its device portfolio. The IPO gave the company a currency for expansion and a public profile in an era when compound semiconductors were attracting serious investment attention. Revenue was still modest — a few tens of millions of dollars — but Cree had established itself as the leading commercial supplier of SiC substrates and a credible player in wide-bandgap LEDs.

## The LED Decades and a Widening Identity, 1993–2017

Through the 1990s and into the 2000s, Cree's blue LED technology evolved from a curiosity into a dominant commercial franchise. The launch of high-brightness blue and then white LEDs — Cree white LEDs achieved record luminous-efficacy figures that the company publicised aggressively — transformed solid-state lighting from a niche application into a credible replacement for fluorescent and incandescent lamps. Charles Swoboda, who became chief executive in 2001, overseeing the company through its most commercially successful period as an LED powerhouse, guided a business that at its peak generated substantial revenue and gross margin from LED components and lighting products sold into commercial, industrial, and consumer channels.

The LED franchise, however, carried a structural tension. SiC's role in LED manufacturing was largely as a substrate for early blue devices; by the mid-2000s, the industry had broadly shifted to gallium nitride on sapphire substrates, where Cree competed as a device-and-module maker rather than as a substrate-materials monopolist. The SiC power-semiconductor opportunity — the original materials insight — was developing slowly but with arguably far greater long-run addressable market, as automotive electrification and industrial power conversion began to demand components that silicon simply could not efficiently provide.

That tension — LED franchise generating today's cash flow, SiC power semiconductors representing tomorrow's strategic position — defined Cree's boardroom debates as the 2010s progressed.

## The Lowe Transformation, 2017–2021

Gregg Lowe arrived as chief executive in September 2017 from NXP Semiconductors, where he had been executive vice-president. His mandate, stated with unusual directness, was to decide what kind of company Cree should be. Within months of taking the role, Lowe had concluded that the LED business, despite its revenue contribution, was a structural distraction — a commoditising market subject to intense Asian competition — and that the company's durable competitive advantage resided in its four-decade mastery of SiC crystal growth and wafer production.

The sequencing of what followed was methodical. In May 2019, Cree announced it had selected a site in Marcy, New York — in the Mohawk Valley — for the world's first purpose-built 200-millimetre SiC wafer fabrication facility, a project eventually described as a multi-billion-dollar investment and positioned as a keystone of American semiconductor industrial policy. The announcement came as electric-vehicle architectures were converging on 800-volt battery systems, which placed SiC MOSFETs at the heart of traction inverter design. Wolfspeed was positioning to be the substrate and device supplier of record for that transition.

In April 2021, Cree completed the divestiture of its LED Products business to SMART Global Holdings, which rebranded the unit as CreeLED. The transaction removed a substantial revenue stream but also removed the management distraction, the capital competition for investment, and the brand identity that tied the company to a commoditising technology. Three months later, in September 2021, the Mohawk Valley fab — christened the "Fastest Fab in the World" in company materials — held its formal groundbreaking. Robert Smith, administrator of the US Small Business Administration, attended; the event signalled the project's alignment with emerging federal policy around domestic semiconductor manufacturing.

On 1 October 2021, Cree, Inc. was officially renamed Wolfspeed, Inc. The new ticker, WOLF, replaced CREE on the New York Stock Exchange. Lowe described the renaming as completing a transformation: the company was now, unambiguously, a silicon carbide power-semiconductor company.

## The RF Divestiture and the Pure-Play Identity, 2023

One business line remained attached to the reconceived identity: SiC RF devices, used in wireless base stations and defence applications, which traced their lineage to Cree's GaN-on-SiC compound semiconductor expertise. In December 2023, Wolfspeed divested that business — branded as Cree/Wolfspeed RF — to MACOM Technology Solutions for $125 million in cash and $50 million in MACOM common stock. The sale closed the loop. From December 2023 onward, Wolfspeed's entire commercial focus was SiC power semiconductors: bare wafers, epitaxial wafers, and power devices. The RF divestiture proceeds provided near-term liquidity, but the underlying financial trajectory was already deteriorating.

## Mohawk Valley Ramp and Financial Deterioration, 2022–2025

The Mohawk Valley fab began producing devices in 2022, a milestone Wolfspeed marked in investor materials as the opening of the first dedicated 200mm SiC fab in the world. The ramp, however, proved far slower and more expensive than the financial model had assumed. Capacity-utilisation underabsorption — the accounting drag of paying for fixed manufacturing costs on a line operating far below target throughput — compressed gross margins severely. Wolfspeed reported revenues in the $750 million to $900 million range against substantial operating losses across the 2022-to-2025 fiscal years, burning cash at a rate that its convertible-note capital structure could not indefinitely support.

EV customer design-in wins — Stellantis, Mercedes-Benz, Lucid Motors among the disclosed relationships — validated the technology thesis but proved slower to convert to volume purchase orders than the company's own ramp schedule had assumed. The EV market itself decelerated in 2023-2024 as consumer adoption plateaued temporarily, reducing the urgency with which Tier-1 automotive suppliers needed to qualify and scale new inverter designs.

Gregg Lowe departed as chief executive in November 2024 after seven years overseeing the transformation from LED company to SiC pure-play. Thomas Werner, a former chief executive of SunPower, stepped in as interim CEO as the company navigated worsening liquidity and creditor negotiations. In May 2025, Robert Feurle — a semiconductor executive with prior leadership roles at Mosaid Technologies and STMicroelectronics — was appointed President and Chief Executive Officer, taking the helm as restructuring discussions advanced toward a formal filing.

## Chapter 11 and the Restructuring Framework, June 2025

In June 2025, Wolfspeed filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in US Bankruptcy Court, initiating a pre-packaged restructuring framework that the company had negotiated with its principal creditors ahead of the filing. The framework contemplated a debt-for-equity exchange that would materially reduce Wolfspeed's balance-sheet debt and allow it to emerge from the Chapter 11 process — targeted for completion in 2025-2026 — as a going concern with continuing operations at Mohawk Valley. The Mohawk Valley fab ramp, the merchant SiC wafer supply business, and the EV and AI power-semiconductor device pipeline were all designated as continuing operations through the restructuring.

The filing was the legal conclusion to a financial trajectory that had been visible in the quarterly disclosures for several years. What it did not resolve, at the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026, was whether the post-emergence capital structure would prove adequate to fund the remaining Mohawk Valley ramp to the utilisation rates at which the fab's unit economics became compelling — the central question on which the investment thesis hinged.

chapters.title: SiC bare wafers, SiC epi, SiC MOSFETs and Schottky diodes, and the vertical value chain
chapters.body:
## The Substrate Foundation

Silicon carbide begins as a boule — a cylindrical crystal grown over days inside a high-temperature furnace at temperatures exceeding 2,000°C. The physics are unforgiving: carbon and silicon atoms must arrange themselves into a hexagonal lattice polytype, predominantly 4H-SiC, with defect densities low enough to support reliable power device operation. Wolfspeed's mastery of this growth process, refined across nearly four decades tracing back to the Cree Research laboratory at North Carolina State University in 1987, constituted the foundational competitive barrier that made everything else in the company's product hierarchy possible.

The company's SiC substrate business produced wafers in two principal geometries through the period ending at the frozen snapshot. The 150mm (six-inch) diameter wafer was the production workhorse through the early 2020s, manufactured principally at the legacy facility in Fayetteville, Arkansas, which Wolfspeed had flagged for phase-out as Mohawk Valley capacity scaled. The 200mm (eight-inch) substrate, meanwhile, represented the strategic pivot: a geometry that would roughly double the usable die area per wafer relative to 150mm, cutting per-unit manufacturing cost at scale and matching the wafer diameter that silicon MOSFET and IGBT fabs had long standardised on. No competitor had demonstrated 200mm SiC in volume production before Wolfspeed opened Mohawk Valley.

The substrate manufacturing sequence proceeded from boule growth through wire-saw slicing, lapping, chemical-mechanical polishing, and epitaxial-ready surface preparation. Wolfspeed's crystal-growth IP — encompassing furnace design, seed crystal preparation, and the thermal-gradient profiles that suppress micropipe and dislocation defects — was the intellectual foundation it had spent decades building. The John W. Pope campus in Saxapahaw, North Carolina became the designated home for expanded boule growth and wafer-slicing capacity tied to the Mohawk Valley device ramp, extending the materials supply chain from crystal to polished substrate within a US domestic footprint.

## Epitaxial Layers: The Performance Interface

Between the substrate and the active device sits the epitaxial layer — a precisely doped, thin crystalline film grown on top of the polished SiC wafer in a chemical vapour deposition reactor. The epi layer's nitrogen-doping concentration and thickness determine the blocking voltage and on-state resistance of the eventual power device; a 1200V MOSFET requires a different epi specification than a 650V device, and a 3300V device for rail traction requires a substantially thicker, more lightly doped layer again.

Wolfspeed manufactured epi wafers both for internal consumption — feeding directly into the Mohawk Valley and legacy Durham device fabrication lines — and as a merchant product sold to external device makers who sourced the SiC substrate and epi stack from Wolfspeed but performed device fabrication in-house. The external epi business served a customer set that overlapped with, but was not identical to, the bare-wafer merchant business: a customer might source bare wafers from Wolfspeed and grow their own epi, or source a completed epi wafer ready for photolithography. The flexibility in offering both options supported customer stickiness while allowing Wolfspeed to capture additional value-chain margin compared with a substrate-only supply relationship.

Epi quality — measured in surface defect density, doping uniformity, and layer thickness variation — was the critical determinant of downstream device yield. Wolfspeed's multi-year investments in epi reactor engineering, run-to-run process control, and defect inspection contributed to the yield economics that underpinned device manufacturing profitability. As Mohawk Valley ramped through 2023 and 2024, epi quality and consistency on 200mm substrates was among the most closely watched technical variables.

## Power Devices: The Revenue Engine

The device product line was where Wolfspeed's substrate and epi manufacturing converted into the power semiconductors that end-customers actually designed into systems. Two product families dominated the discrete power device revenue.

**SiC MOSFETs** spanned a voltage range from 650V through 3300V, covering essentially the full spectrum of medium-to-high-voltage power conversion. The 650V and 750V classes addressed solar microinverters, EV on-board chargers, and server power-supply units — applications where GaN also competed but SiC offered advantages at higher current levels. The 1200V class was the automotive traction inverter workhorse, designed into EV platforms from Stellantis, Mercedes-Benz, and a broader Tier-1 automotive supplier base that was still converting design-in wins into volume shipments through the 2024-2025 period. The 1700V class addressed industrial motor drives, wind turbine converters, and medium-voltage industrial applications. The 3300V class targeted rail traction systems and high-power industrial converters where silicon IGBTs had traditionally dominated and SiC offered efficiency and switching-frequency advantages.

**SiC Schottky diodes** served as both standalone products and as companion devices within SiC MOSFET power modules. Operating as the freewheeling diode in a half-bridge switching stage, a SiC Schottky diode eliminated the reverse recovery charge losses that afflicted silicon p-n diodes, enabling higher switching frequencies and reduced passive component sizing. Wolfspeed's Schottky diode portfolio, spanning voltage classes broadly aligned with the MOSFET range, had been in production longer than the MOSFET portfolio and represented a mature, defensible revenue line even as MOSFETs attracted most of the design-win narrative.

Both device families were packaged in industry-standard TO-247, D2PAK, and surface-mount packages for discrete sales, and in bare-die form for customer assembly into power modules. The packaging choice reflected end-market segmentation: discrete-packaged devices for lower-current point-of-load and auxiliary applications, bare die for automotive-grade modules assembled by Tier-1 power module manufacturers.

## Mohawk Valley: The 200mm Bet

The Marcy, New York facility — marketed under the Mohawk Valley banner — was the largest capital-investment programme in Wolfspeed's history and arguably the most consequential single manufacturing facility investment in the global SiC industry. When the fab broke ground and began initial qualification in 2022, it represented the first dedicated 200mm SiC device fabrication facility anywhere in the world. Silicon fabs had long operated at 300mm; SiC remained years behind, and Wolfspeed elected to skip the intermediate 200mm silicon-equivalent learning curve that its competitors were still navigating at 150mm.

Total capital deployed across the Mohawk Valley project through 2025 ran into multiple billions of dollars. The facility was designed for SiC MOSFET fabrication using 200mm wafers, employing deep-ultraviolet lithography and advanced etch, implant, and metallisation processes adapted from silicon CMOS but engineered for SiC's harder, more chemically resistant crystal. The New York State Thruway corridor location was not accidental: state economic development incentives, proximity to existing semiconductor supply chains, and the political alignment with US domestic semiconductor manufacturing strategy under the CHIPS and Science Act all contributed to the site selection.

Ramp execution at Mohawk Valley proved harder than the 2021-era investor presentations implied. Yield improvement on 200mm SiC was slower than plan, and capacity utilisation underabsorption generated the fixed-cost headwinds that dominated Wolfspeed's income statement through fiscal years 2023, 2024, and into 2025. The underabsorption dynamic was mechanical: a multi-billion-dollar fab carrying high depreciation and operating costs against a production volume that had not yet reached the utilisation levels where unit economics turn positive. Management characterised the ramp trajectory on successive earnings calls, with Gregg Lowe describing the progression in incremental utilisation milestones before his departure in November 2024.

The CHIPS Act engagement added a strategic dimension to the Mohawk Valley financing picture. US Department of Commerce announcements through 2024 and into 2025 identified Wolfspeed among domestic semiconductor manufacturers targeted for CHIPS Act support, though the precise disbursement schedule and conditions remained subject to verification against 8-K disclosures at the snapshot date. The award, if and when disbursed, was expected to partially offset the capital requirements of the Mohawk Valley ramp and the associated Saxapahaw materials expansion.

## The Vertical Integration Thesis

| Value-chain layer | Wolfspeed asset | Geography |
|---|---|---|
| SiC boule growth | John W. Pope Saxapahaw expansion | Saxapahaw, North Carolina |
| Wafer slicing and polishing | Saxapahaw; legacy Fayetteville (phasing) | North Carolina; Arkansas |
| Epitaxial growth | Research Triangle Park; Mohawk Valley | Durham NC; Marcy NY |
| Device fabrication (200mm) | Mohawk Valley | Marcy, New York |
| Device fabrication (150mm legacy) | Research Triangle Park | Durham, North Carolina |
| Merchant substrate supply | External — Infineon, STMicro, onsemi, Rohm, Bosch | Customer fabs globally |

The logic of vertical integration ran from cost control to competitive insulation. A device competitor sourcing SiC substrates from the merchant market faced Wolfspeed as both supplier and rival; the substrate customer relationship provided Wolfspeed revenue and customer intelligence while the device business competed for the same end sockets. Wolfspeed management consistently described the vertical model as a source of structural cost advantage at scale — once Mohawk Valley reached target utilisation, the internal transfer price from the Saxapahaw substrate operation to the Mohawk Valley device fab would reflect a cost structure unavailable to fabless or fab-light competitors sourcing substrates externally.

## Merchant Wafer Supply: Revenue and Intelligence

The external substrate and epi wafer business was not incidental to the Wolfspeed model. Selling SiC substrates to Infineon, STMicroelectronics, onsemi, Bosch, and Rohm — each a competitor in the SiC device market — generated revenue that contributed to Wolfspeed's materials-segment economics while the device segment remained capital-intensive and loss-generating. The merchant supply relationships also provided a form of industry signalling: volumes purchased, specifications requested, and qualification cycles initiated conveyed information about where competitors were in their own device roadmaps.

The merchant substrate business carried inherent tension. Customers who depended on Wolfspeed substrates had strategic incentives to diversify supply — Infineon's acquisition of Siltectra and investments in SiC substrate capability reflected precisely this logic. At the same time, Wolfspeed's multi-decade process lead at 150mm and its 200mm substrate qualification progress gave it a technical position that alternatives struggled to replicate quickly. The June 2025 Chapter 11 filing introduced a new dimension of customer concern: would substrates continue to flow reliably from a company in bankruptcy proceedings? The pre-packaged restructuring framework, with its focus on operational continuity through emergence, was designed in part to address that question before it became a customer-retention crisis.

chapters.title: Revenue trajectory, Mohawk Valley capex, Chapter 11 restructuring, post-emergence capital structure
chapters.body:
## The Revenue Plateau and Margin Collapse

Wolfspeed's four-year revenue record between fiscal 2022 and fiscal 2025 — fiscal years running from late June to late June — describes a company that achieved modest growth but never achieved profitability, and that watched its gross-margin structure buckle under the weight of a capital investment it had made before its end markets were ready to absorb the output.

In [fiscal 2022, ended June 26, 2022](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000895419&type=10-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=40), the first complete annual period under the Wolfspeed name and the first with the LED segment fully divested, the company disclosed revenue of approximately $746 million. That figure reflected the two principal segments — Power Products (SiC devices) and Materials (SiC substrates and epi wafers) — against a backdrop of accelerating design-in activity and bullish commentary from management about the EV traction inverter opportunity. In the [fiscal 2023 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000895419&type=10-K), revenue grew to approximately $807 million, a year-on-year increase of roughly eight percent driven by early Mohawk Valley device ramp-up and continued materials demand from merchant wafer customers including Infineon Technologies, STMicroelectronics, onsemi, and Rohm.

Fiscal 2024 (ended June 30, 2024) was where the revenue plateau materialised. Despite ambitious guidance issued at the start of that year, broad-based customer push-outs in the automotive segment — driven by slower-than-projected EV adoption rates and Tier-1 supplier inventory corrections — meant top-line performance came in roughly flat versus fiscal 2023, inside the $800 million range. At the same time the cost structure had grown dramatically: Mohawk Valley was consuming capital at a rate of roughly $1 billion or more per year in capex, and depreciation charges were accelerating as the facility reached commercial scale. Fiscal 2025 (ended approximately June 29, 2025) saw revenue decline further from the plateau as automotive design-in volumes failed to convert to purchase orders at the projected cadence, pulling the full-year figure back toward the lower bound of the $750 million–$900 million range disclosed across the period.

| Fiscal Year | Period End | Revenue (approx.) | YoY Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | June 26, 2022 | ~$746M | — |
| FY2023 | June 25, 2023 | ~$807M | +8% |
| FY2024 | June 30, 2024 | ~$807M | Flat |
| FY2025 | ~June 29, 2025 | ~$750M (est.) | ~−7% |

*Sources: [WOLF 10-K filings, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000895419&type=10-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=40)*

## Mohawk Valley: The Capex Wager and the Underabsorption Problem

The Mohawk Valley facility in Marcy, New York — inaugurated as the first dedicated 200mm SiC fab in the world — sits at the centre of Wolfspeed's financial deterioration and its forward investment thesis in equal measure. The total project cost, inclusive of equipment procurement, cleanroom fit-out, and supporting infrastructure, represented the single largest capital project in the company's history and among the largest dedicated SiC manufacturing investments globally, with public disclosures pointing toward a multi-billion-dollar all-in figure before federal and state offsets.

Annual capital expenditure at its peak exceeded $1 billion, concentrated principally in fiscal years 2022 through 2024. The cumulative capex deployed at Mohawk Valley — combined with continued investment in the John W. Pope materials campus in Saxapahaw, North Carolina — placed extraordinary demands on the balance sheet and financing capacity. [CHIPS Act funding](https://www.commerce.gov/chips) was always integral to the Mohawk Valley financial model. In early 2024, the US Department of Commerce announced a preliminary term sheet providing Wolfspeed with up to approximately $750 million in direct CHIPS Act funding under the Creating Helpful Incentives to Produce Semiconductors Act, a figure conditioned on continued investment execution and ramp milestones. New York State economic development commitments from Empire State Development provided a further capital offset, underwriting a portion of the Marcy site and infrastructure costs.

The core financial problem was utilisation. Mohawk Valley entered commercial operation with a nameplate capacity that far exceeded near-term demand, and the accounting consequences were immediate and severe. Manufacturing overhead — depreciation on cleanroom equipment, facility costs, and direct labour — must be absorbed against units of production. When a factory operates at low single-digit or low-teen utilisation rates, as Mohawk Valley did through fiscal 2023 and much of fiscal 2024, unabsorbed overhead flows directly to cost of goods sold rather than being capitalised into inventory, collapsing the reported gross margin.

The GAAP gross-margin impact was documented explicitly in the fiscal 2023 and fiscal 2024 10-K disclosures. Non-GAAP gross margin — excluding stock-based compensation and certain one-time items — was running in the low-to-mid-twenty percent range on the underlying device business; GAAP gross margin, inclusive of Mohawk Valley underabsorption charges, was substantially negative. The gap between the two metrics, sometimes spanning twenty percentage points or more, illustrated how decisively the ramp was destroying reported profitability even as management maintained the underlying economics of the device business remained sound.

Then-CEO Gregg Lowe defended the strategy consistently through fiscal 2023 and into fiscal 2024, describing the investment as a "once-in-a-generation opportunity" and noting on earnings calls that the company had accumulated an $18 billion design-in pipeline providing, in his framing, line of sight to future revenue that would ultimately fill the Mohawk Valley capacity. The characterisation grew harder to sustain as automotive OEM push-outs accumulated through calendar 2024.

## The Operating Loss Spiral

Operating losses compounded through the period. In [fiscal 2023](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000895419&type=10-K), the GAAP operating loss approached approximately $474 million, driven by Mohawk Valley underabsorption charges, elevated research-and-development expense, and stock-based compensation — all overlaid on a revenue base that had not yet grown large enough to defray the fixed-cost load. By fiscal 2024 the operating loss had widened further, with depreciation charges escalating as equipment placed into service in prior years moved into full amortisation cycles. Research-and-development investment was sustained through the period as the company advanced 200mm device process development and next-generation materials work.

The combination — high fixed costs, low utilisation, flat revenue, and a debt-service burden growing in line with successive capital raises — produced cash burn of a severity that progressively narrowed the liquidity runway. Free cash flow was deeply negative in each of fiscal years 2022 through 2025. Working-capital dynamics provided limited buffer: customer advance payments and long-term supply agreements with automotive customers had bolstered the balance sheet in earlier periods, but as push-outs mounted those prepayments were consumed and not renewed at scale.

Gregg Lowe departed as CEO in November 2024, succeeded by Thomas Werner on an interim basis. Robert Feurle, with prior executive experience at Mosaid and STMicroelectronics, was appointed President and Chief Executive Officer in May 2025, explicitly as the leader to navigate the Chapter 11 process and steward the post-emergence company.

## The Pre-Petition Capital Structure

The debt stack that accumulated to finance the Mohawk Valley ramp was the proximate cause of the June 2025 petition. By the time of filing, Wolfspeed carried a total funded-debt burden in the range of approximately $2.7 billion to $3 billion, composed of several layers with varying maturities and seniority.

The principal instruments included multiple tranches of convertible senior notes — among them approximately $750 million in 1.875% convertible notes due 2029 and approximately $460 million in zero-coupon convertible notes due 2026 — alongside other convertible tranches and a secured revolving credit facility. The convertible note stack had been structured to provide financing flexibility at a time when equity-market enthusiasm for the SiC structural story remained elevated; as the WOLF share price declined from post-renaming peaks toward distressed territory, the embedded conversion options became economically irrelevant, and the notes traded closer to their principal value as straight debt instruments. Debt-service obligations were running at levels the operating business could not sustain from operations, and the prospect of the 2026 maturity wall — with a rolling challenge into the 2029 notes — made a liability-management exercise inevitable.

## June 2025: The Pre-Packaged Chapter 11 Framework

The Chapter 11 petition, filed in the United States Bankruptcy Court in June 2025, was a pre-packaged or pre-arranged restructuring: Wolfspeed had reached agreement with a substantial majority of its major creditors on the key terms of a plan of reorganisation before formally entering the court process. A pre-packaged structure is materially faster than a contested reorganisation, and management and its advisers anticipated that a pre-packaged plan could proceed through confirmation and emergence within months rather than years.

The central mechanism was a debt-for-equity exchange. Holders of the convertible senior notes and other unsecured debt instruments agreed to exchange their principal claims for equity in the reorganised entity, substantially eliminating the pre-petition funded debt from the post-emergence balance sheet. Senior secured creditors were expected to receive recovery at or near par; convertible noteholders — whose instruments had traded well below par in the months preceding the filing — would receive equity representing a pro-rata share of the reorganised company at a negotiated enterprise valuation. Pre-petition common stockholders faced substantial or near-total dilution, as is standard in debt-heavy pre-packaged restructurings where enterprise value is insufficient to support a meaningful residual equity claim.

| Instrument | Approximate Principal | Restructuring Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Convertible senior notes (multiple tranches) | ~$2.0B–$2.3B | Debt-for-equity exchange |
| Senior secured revolving facility | Variable | Recovery at or near par |
| Other pre-petition obligations | Residual | Per plan of reorganisation |
| Pre-petition WOLF common equity | — | Diluted to de minimis / cancelled |

*Sources: [WOLF 8-K filings, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000895419&type=8-K); US Bankruptcy Court docket (PACER)*

Operating continuity through the Chapter 11 period was preserved via a debtor-in-possession financing arrangement providing the liquidity necessary to sustain Mohawk Valley operations, pay employees, and meet supplier obligations across the reorganisation window.

## CHIPS Act, Post-Emergence Capital Structure, and the Forward Equation

The post-emergence balance sheet was designed to be materially deleveraged versus the pre-petition structure. With the convertible note stack converted to equity, the reorganised Wolfspeed was targeted to emerge carrying substantially reduced funded debt — and with the CHIPS Act award, if and when disbursed in accordance with the Department of Commerce milestone schedule, providing a significant non-dilutive capital infusion to sustain continued Mohawk Valley investment.

The disbursement of the preliminary $750 million CHIPS Act award was subject to formal definitive agreement execution and ongoing milestone verification, stages that were still proceeding through the frozen-window date of May 23, 2026. New York State commitments from Empire State Development provided a further layer of capital support, having underwritten a portion of the Marcy site and infrastructure costs that reduced the net company-funded capex obligation.

The post-emergence financial model hinges on a single variable above all others: the rate at which Mohawk Valley utilisation improves. Each incremental percentage point of utilisation converts previously unabsorbed overhead into product margin, producing an operating-leverage effect that is unusually steep for a capital-intensive manufacturer. At utilisation rates approaching 40 to 50 percent — still well below full capacity — the facility's gross-margin contribution would begin to inflect toward positive GAAP territory, fundamentally altering the company's cash-consumption profile. Achieving that inflection requires automotive customers to absorb contracted volumes, which in turn requires EV production to continue growing and design-in victories at Stellantis, Mercedes-Benz, and the broader Tier-1 base to convert to sustained purchase-order flow. It also requires the emerging AI data-centre 800V HVDC architecture — where SiC MOSFETs serve high-voltage power-conversion stages at hyperscaler facilities — to grow fast enough to supplement automotive demand during any continued EV-cycle softness.

The June 2025 Chapter 11 process was, in this framing, not a liquidation but an acknowledgement that the gap between the investment cycle and the revenue cycle was simply too wide for the pre-petition balance sheet to bridge. The debt-for-equity exchange gave the company a second balance sheet — one capable, in principle, of surviving the remaining years of the Mohawk Valley utilisation ramp without the weight of nearly $3 billion in funded debt pressing against every operating quarter and every earnings release.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
## The Complication of Valuing a Restructuring Pure-Play

Conventional equity valuation frameworks break down when applied to Wolfspeed at the frozen snapshot of May 23, 2026. The company filed for Chapter 11 protection in June 2025, a pre-packaged restructuring premised on debt-for-equity exchange with consenting creditors. Common equity — the traded WOLF share on the NYSE — effectively ceased to convey meaningful enterprise ownership once the restructuring framework was confirmed; in Chapter 11, common shareholders sit below all creditor claims, and in a balance-sheet-insolvent restructuring the residual equity value in existing shares approaches zero. Trailing and forward price-to-earnings multiples are therefore uninformative: Wolfspeed has generated no net income, and the earnings-per-share denominator is itself being renegotiated.

The analytically useful lens is enterprise value relative to revenue — EV/Sales — supplemented by a post-emergence scenario framework that asks what the reorganized entity is worth once the capital structure is repaired. That framing is what the rest of this chapter pursues.

## From $20 Billion to Zero: A De-Rating in Four Chapters

The arc of Wolfspeed's multiple history encapsulates the full SiC hype cycle. At its peak in November 2021 — shortly after the October 2021 renaming from Cree to Wolfspeed and amid peak EV investor enthusiasm — the stock reached approximately $142 per share. With roughly 125 to 127 million diluted shares outstanding and approximately $3 billion in gross debt at the time, the enterprise value was in the range of $18 to $21 billion. Revenue for the fiscal year ending late June 2022 was broadly in the $700 million range, implying a peak EV/Sales multiple of approximately 25 to 30 times — a valuation that embedded not just growth but the entire SiC structural thesis at once.

The first de-rating phase, spanning late 2022 through 2023, reflected the collision of execution reality with that thesis. Mohawk Valley's 200mm SiC fab came online but ramp pace disappointed; capacity-utilization underabsorption produced gross margins that were deeply negative at the fab level; and EV production ramp deferrals by European and North American OEMs pushed out the revenue conversion that design-in wins had promised. By mid-2023 the stock had retreated to the $30 to $40 range, implying EV/Sales in the 5 to 7 times range — still pricing in substantial growth recovery.

The second de-rating, through 2024, was driven by the accumulating weight of the balance sheet. Long-term debt — principally convertible notes — had grown to approximately $4 to $5 billion, a figure that dwarfed revenue. As the likelihood of a restructuring became visible in SEC disclosures and credit-market spreads, equity value collapsed toward optionality. By early 2025 the stock was in the $4 to $6 range. With 127 million shares, the market capitalization was roughly $500 to $750 million; adding the debt load yielded a nominal enterprise value of $4.5 to $5.5 billion — still 5 to 7 times the roughly $800 million revenue run-rate, because the debt was real even when the equity was not. That apparently stubborn EV/Sales figure is an artifact of leverage, not a genuine premium.

The June 2025 Chapter 11 filing extinguished the residual equity value. The third and fourth chapters are being written in the restructuring court and in the Mohawk Valley fab simultaneously.

## Peer-Group Multiple Comparison

The table below compares Wolfspeed's pre-distress and post-emergence estimated multiples against the principal named SiC and compound-semiconductor power peers, using approximate figures as of or around the frozen snapshot. Wolfspeed multiples are presented as a post-emergence scenario range rather than a live market quote, for the reasons described above.

| Company | Ticker | Revenue Scale | EV/Sales (approx.) | EV/EBITDA | P/E (NTM) | SiC Revenue Exposure |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wolfspeed (post-emergence est.) | WOLF | ~$800M–$1B | 2.0–3.5× | N/M (pre-profit) | N/M | 100% pure-play |
| onsemi | ON | ~$6–7B | 3.0–4.5× | 12–18× | 18–25× | ~25–30% |
| Infineon Technologies | IFX.DE | ~$15–17B | 2.0–3.0× | 10–15× | 18–24× | ~20% |
| STMicroelectronics | STM | ~$13–15B | 1.5–2.5× | 8–13× | 12–18× | ~15% |
| Rohm Semiconductor | 6963.T | ~$3–4B | 1.0–2.0× | 10–14× | 20–28× | ~20–25% |
| Coherent Corp | COHR | ~$5–6B | 1.5–2.5× | 12–18× | N/M–25× | <10% |

*Note: All figures are approximations based on publicly disclosed financials and analyst consensus estimates available at or before the frozen snapshot. Post-emergence Wolfspeed figures are scenario-derived rather than market-quoted.*

The peer group reveals a structural discount problem: even the most optimistic post-emergence EV/Sales assignment for Wolfspeed — 3.5 times on $900 million in revenue — yields a gross enterprise value of roughly $3.1 billion. Against estimated reorganized debt of $1.0 to $1.5 billion (reflecting the debt-for-equity conversion framework), the implied equity is $1.6 to $2.1 billion. That is a fraction of the $18 billion peak and still contingent on execution that has not yet been demonstrated at scale.

## Intrinsic Value: What Cash-Flow Trajectory Does the Current Implied Enterprise Value Embed?

A simplified DCF framing anchors the discussion. If one assigns a post-emergence enterprise value of $2 billion — the rough midpoint of the scenario range — and assumes a terminal EBITDA margin of 20 percent (a reasonable steady-state for a scaled SiC device manufacturer with a captive substrate supply chain), the implied revenue at terminal value must be approximately $1.5 to $2.0 billion to justify that enterprise value at a 10 to 12 times terminal EBITDA multiple. That revenue figure requires Wolfspeed to nearly double from its current run-rate, which in turn requires Mohawk Valley to reach meaningful utilization — likely 60 to 70 percent of nameplate capacity — and the EV and industrial design-in book to convert to production volumes.

The discount rate applied to this trajectory is itself elevated. A freshly emerged Chapter 11 company with a manufacturing ramp in progress, a management team installed mid-restructuring, and a competitive set that includes heavily capitalized European and Japanese incumbents carries execution risk that a standard 10 percent WACC understates. At a 14 to 16 percent discount rate — appropriate for a restructured single-site pure-play semiconductor company — the present value of that terminal horizon falls materially, and the margin for execution error narrows to near zero.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

**Bull case — $3.0 to $3.5 billion enterprise value, implied equity $1.5 to $2.5 billion:** Mohawk Valley reaches 65 percent utilization by the end of calendar 2026, gross margins turn positive at the device level, and the EV SiC design-in book — principally Stellantis, Mercedes-Benz, and broader European Tier-1s — begins volume shipments on schedule. AI data center 800V HVDC exposure adds an incremental high-ASP revenue layer. CHIPS Act disbursements arrive without conditionality delays, reducing post-emergence refinancing risk. The multiple assumed: 3.5 times EV/Sales on $900 million to $1 billion revenue, in line with onsemi's current rating when its SiC ramp was gaining traction. This scenario requires everything to proceed without further slippage in either the fab ramp or the EV demand cycle.

**Base case — $1.8 to $2.2 billion enterprise value, implied equity $0.6 to $1.2 billion:** Mohawk Valley exits 2026 at 45 to 55 percent utilization — meaningful progress but short of breakeven on the marginal cost structure. Revenue grows modestly toward $850 to $900 million. EBITDA remains slightly negative or at breakeven. The appropriate multiple is approximately 2.0 to 2.5 times EV/Sales, reflecting a company that has demonstrated it can execute but has not yet earned the growth premium. Post-emergence debt of roughly $1.2 billion implies equity of $600 million to $1 billion — real value for creditors who took the restructuring risk, but a sobering outcome relative to the original equity base.

**Bear case — $1.0 to $1.3 billion enterprise value, implied equity near zero to $300 million:** Mohawk Valley ramp encounters further yield or equipment setbacks. EV SiC volumes soften again as OEMs defer inverter platform launches. The AI data center SiC opportunity develops slower than anticipated, and CHIPS Act funding is delayed by condition precedents. Revenue slips toward $750 to $780 million. At 1.5 times EV/Sales the enterprise value falls to roughly $1.1 to $1.2 billion. Against $1.2 billion in reorganized debt, equity is nominal or negative — a scenario in which even creditors who accepted deep haircuts in the restructuring find themselves underwater.

## What the Market Has Priced In

The honest read, at the frozen snapshot, is that the market for Wolfspeed's reorganized equity does not yet exist in a form that allows clean price discovery. Former WOLF common equity is effectively cancelled. New equity issued in the restructuring to creditors will reflect the valuation negotiated in the Chapter 11 plan — a number driven by the enterprise value agreed between the company and its principal creditors, not by open-market discovery. That negotiated enterprise value is itself constrained by the need to give creditors a credible recovery while leaving Wolfspeed with enough equity cushion to raise capital for the ongoing Mohawk Valley ramp.

The gap between the dossier's read and any implied consensus is therefore less about multiple disagreement and more about execution probability. The base case enterprise value of $2 billion is defensible if Wolfspeed executes. The history of the Mohawk Valley ramp — repeated utilization-guidance cuts, CEO turnover at the worst possible moment, and a balance sheet that offered no buffer against demand-cycle softness — argues for assigning material probability to the bear case. The bull case requires a confluence of favorable outcomes that has not characterized any stage of Wolfspeed's post-renaming history. Until Mohawk Valley posts two consecutive quarters of utilization above 50 percent with confirmed device gross-margin improvement, the base case should be held lightly and the bear tail weighted accordingly.

chapters.title: Quarterly cadence through Mohawk Valley ramp, financial deterioration, and Chapter 11
chapters.body:
## From Cree to Wolfspeed: The Wager on Silicon Carbide

When Wolfspeed held its October 2021 rebrand ceremony, retiring the Cree name that had anchored a Research Triangle Park success story for three decades, the symbolism was deliberate. The company had already divested its LED component business to SMART Global Holdings earlier that year, completing a strategic pivot that Gregg Lowe—who arrived from Texas Instruments as CEO in 2017—had spent four years engineering. What remained was a pure-play silicon carbide company, listed on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker WOLF, betting that the electrification of transportation would generate insatiable demand for SiC power devices capable of handling the high-voltage switching loads that silicon MOSFETs could not efficiently manage.

The pivot's financial architecture was straightforward in theory and punishing in practice: borrow heavily, build the world's largest 200mm SiC wafer fabrication facility, achieve scale economies that Durham's legacy 150mm lines could never match, and ride the EV adoption curve to profitability. Through fiscal years 2022 to 2025—ending each late June—that thesis was stress-tested against a slowing EV demand cycle, persistent fab underutilization, and a capital structure that left no room for the ramp to take longer than the bond market would permit.

## FY2022: Groundbreaking and the Mohawk Valley Commitment

Wolfspeed's fiscal year 2022, which ended in late June 2022, was defined by construction rather than production. The company broke ground on the John Palmour Manufacturing Center for Silicon Carbide in Marcy, New York—in the Mohawk Valley outside Utica—in April 2022, committing to what management described as the industry's first 200mm SiC fab at commercial scale. Total project investment was projected to reach roughly $1 billion for the initial phase, with expansion pathways extending toward a multi-billion-dollar campus over the decade.

Full-year revenue for FY2022 came in near $746 million, with the company reporting GAAP operating losses running into the hundreds of millions as research and development intensity increased alongside pre-ramp capital expenditure. On the Durham, North Carolina, 150mm lines, the company was generating device revenue, but gross margins were constrained by startup costs, yield development work on SiC epitaxy, and the overhead absorption challenge of running two simultaneous fab programs.

Design-in wins were the narrative currency of this period. Lowe and his team regularly cited the company's "design-in pipeline"—the dollar value of future device revenue from programs where Wolfspeed MOSFETs or Schottky diodes had been selected by automotive Tier-1s or OEMs for vehicles still in development—as evidence that the revenue backlog justified the capital program. By early FY2023, that pipeline figure had grown to tens of billions of dollars in lifetime contract value, a metric that shaped investor sentiment even as near-term losses widened.

## FY2023: Peak Revenue and the RF Exit

Fiscal year 2023 brought Wolfspeed's highest annual revenue of the period under review, reaching approximately $891 million as the company captured incremental SiC device demand while still operating from its 150mm Durham lines at capacity. The Mohawk Valley facility was mid-construction; the company had not yet begun qualifying devices from the new fab.

In December 2023—technically the second quarter of FY2024—Wolfspeed completed the sale of its RF business to MACOM Technology Solutions for approximately $75 million in cash plus potential earnout consideration. The transaction shed the gallium nitride RF product line, which served defense and wireless infrastructure customers, and which Wolfspeed's management judged non-core relative to the EV and industrial power-device opportunity. The divestiture freed engineering focus but was not large enough to materially alter the capital structure.

More significant was the macroeconomic turn that emerged through calendar 2023. Electric vehicle adoption in North America and Europe decelerated from its 2022-to-early-2023 growth trajectory. Major OEMs, including Ford and General Motors, publicly revised electrification production schedules. For SiC suppliers, the consequence was direct: customers began stretching delivery timelines on existing purchase agreements and reducing near-term order placement. Wolfspeed's design-in pipeline remained nominally intact, but the conversion from design win to volume production revenue—always a multiyear process—was moving further right on the timeline.

## FY2024: Mohawk Valley Opens, Utilization Collapses

The fiscal year ending June 2024 marked both the operational opening of Mohawk Valley and the onset of the company's most acute financial crisis before bankruptcy. The facility began producing devices—the first 200mm SiC wafers in commercial production anywhere in the world, as Wolfspeed's communications emphasized—but ramp velocity was constrained by the simultaneous challenges of yield qualification, customer qualification cycles, and a demand environment that offered limited pull from the automotive sector.

Capacity underabsorption became the dominant line item in the company's cost structure. A semiconductor fab running below its designed utilization rate cannot spread fixed overhead across a sufficient volume of output; the result is a per-unit cost that far exceeds the designed cost model. Mohawk Valley's economics required throughput that the demand environment, in fiscal 2024, would not yet provide. Wolfspeed reported annual revenue of approximately $807 million for FY2024—below the FY2023 peak—and GAAP operating losses that reflected not only the continuing R&D and SG&A burden but the Mohawk Valley underabsorption charge.

A significant offsetting signal arrived in February 2024, when the US Department of Commerce announced a preliminary memorandum of terms under the CHIPS and Science Act, offering Wolfspeed approximately $750 million in direct funding to support the Mohawk Valley expansion and a planned second facility. The announcement provided a public endorsement of the company's strategic position and offered potential relief to the capital structure, but the final grant agreement had not been executed by the close of the fiscal year, leaving the funding contingent on due diligence and negotiation timelines that would carry into the Chapter 11 period.

## The Leadership Transition

In November 2024, Gregg Lowe departed the company he had spent seven years transforming. The board named Thomas Werner—formerly Chief Executive of solar energy company SunPower—as interim President and CEO. Werner's appointment was explicitly transitional; the board disclosed it was conducting a formal search for a permanent successor.

The interim period ran through the winter and spring of 2025 as the company continued to report quarterly results reflecting declining revenue, persistent underutilization charges, and a capital structure increasingly viewed by the debt markets as unsustainable. Wolfspeed's convertible notes and term loan obligations represented a debt load that operating cash flow, even under an optimistic ramp scenario, could not service on its original schedule.

In May 2025, the board appointed Robert Feurle as President and Chief Executive Officer. Feurle brought a career in power semiconductors with prior roles at STMicroelectronics—one of Wolfspeed's primary SiC competitors—and Mosaid Technologies. His selection signaled that the board and principal creditors who had by then accumulated significant influence over the restructuring process wanted operational semiconductor expertise in the chief executive seat for the Chapter 11 period and post-emergence execution.

## Chapter 11 and the Restructuring Framework

Wolfspeed filed for protection under Chapter 11 of the United States Bankruptcy Code in June 2025—within weeks of Feurle's appointment. The filing, made in a US Bankruptcy Court, was accompanied by a restructuring support agreement executed with a substantial majority of the company's secured and unsecured creditors, establishing the framework for a prepackaged or prearranged reorganization. The proposed plan provided for a debt-for-equity exchange in which holders of the company's outstanding notes and term loan obligations would convert their claims into equity in the reorganized company, materially reducing the funded debt load and providing the post-emergence Wolfspeed with the balance sheet capacity its operations had lacked.

The restructuring framework preserved the Mohawk Valley facility, the Durham wafer operations, and the continuing CHIPS Act funding negotiation as going-concern assets. Management's stated objective was to emerge from Chapter 11 with a capital structure calibrated to the time horizon of the Mohawk Valley ramp—a process that, as the quarterly cadence from FY2022 through FY2025 demonstrated, demanded years of below-utilization operation before the fab's designed unit economics could be achieved.

The company's trajectory from Cree's founding in 1987 through the LED divestiture, the Wolfspeed rename, the Mohawk Valley construction cycle, and the June 2025 Chapter 11 filing described an arc familiar in semiconductor history: a pioneer technology company that correctly identified a structural shift in device demand, built ahead of the cycle, and encountered the timing mismatch between capital deployment and revenue conversion that the capital markets, ultimately, would not absorb.

chapters.title: Robert Feurle, Thomas Werner, Gregg Lowe legacy, CFO, executive team, and the board
chapters.body:
## The Founding Generation

Wolfspeed's leadership history begins at North Carolina State University in 1987, when brothers F. Neal Hunter and Eric Hunter incorporated Cree Research, a venture built on proprietary silicon carbide crystal-growth technology developed in the university's laboratories. The company went public on NASDAQ in 1993 and over the following two decades built a compound-semiconductor franchise spanning SiC substrates, GaN-on-SiC radio-frequency devices, and — most lucratively for much of its life — blue and white LED chips. Neal Hunter served as chief executive through 2001, succeeded by Charles Swoboda, who ran the company from 2001 until 2017. Under Swoboda, Cree became a NASDAQ component and the dominant name in high-brightness LEDs, even as the LED commodity crash of the 2010s eroded margins and forced the company to look beyond lighting for its next act.

## The Lowe Decade: Transformation, Ambition, and Collapse

The board recruited Gregg Lowe as president and chief executive, effective [September 27, 2017](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000895419/000119312517264869/), replacing Swoboda after a prolonged search for a leader who could execute a hardware-heavy industrial pivot. Lowe arrived from Freescale Semiconductor, where he had served as president and chief executive from 2012 to 2015, running a $5 billion revenue company with 17,000 employees across automotive, industrial, consumer, and communications markets before NXP Semiconductors acquired Freescale in 2015. Before Freescale, Lowe had spent 27 years at Texas Instruments, rising to senior vice president and manager of the Analog Business and playing a central role in TI's acquisition of National Semiconductor. He held a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from Rose-Hulman Institute of Technology and had completed an executive program at Stanford.

Lowe's strategic logic was unambiguous: jettison the commoditising LED business and concentrate entirely on silicon carbide power semiconductors, where Cree's vertical integration — boule growth, wafer slicing, epitaxy, and device fabrication — was defensible against Asian competition in ways that LED chips were not. Execution unfolded in three moves. In 2021, Cree sold its LED lighting and components business to SMART Global Holdings as CreeLED. In October 2021, the company renamed itself Wolfspeed, Inc. to signal the pure-play SiC identity to investors. In December 2023, it divested the residual SiC radio-frequency business — the former Cree RF unit — to MACOM Technology Solutions for $125 million in cash and $50 million in MACOM stock, completing the transformation.

The centrepiece of Lowe's tenure was the Mohawk Valley Fab, a purpose-built 200mm SiC wafer fabrication facility in Marcy, New York — the first such dedicated plant in the world. The project required multi-billion dollars in capital expenditure across 2022 through 2025 and was anchored by a Department of Commerce CHIPS Act award and state-level New York incentives. Strategically, the bet was sound: 200mm SiC wafers offered roughly 1.8 times the die-per-wafer count of the 150mm baseline, a unit-cost advantage essential for competing in EV traction inverters at automotive volume. Operationally, the ramp proved punishing. Yield improvement at 200mm lagged internal targets, design-in customers including Stellantis and Mercedes-Benz faced their own EV volume pullbacks, and the revenue required to service a rapidly expanding debt load never materialised on schedule.

By November 2024, Wolfspeed carried approximately $6.7 billion in funded debt — senior secured notes, convertible notes, and related obligations — against revenue running well below levels needed to service it. The board moved decisively. On November 12, 2024, directors voted to [terminate Lowe's employment without cause](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000895419/000119312524260426/). He stepped down as president, chief executive, and director on November 18, departing the company entirely by the end of that month. In a detail that captured the straitened circumstances, Lowe voluntarily waived the lump-sum payment equal to 1.5 times his target bonus that his change-in-control agreement would otherwise have provided. He subsequently joined the board of Power Integrations in February 2025.

## The Werner Interregnum

The board did not appoint an outside successor immediately. Instead, it turned to Thomas H. Werner, who had served on the Wolfspeed board since March 2006 — an 18-year directorship that encompassed the entire arc from mid-Swoboda Cree through the Wolfspeed transformation — and who had become chairman in October 2023. On November 18, 2024, Werner was named [Executive Chairman](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000895419/000119312524260426/d915019dex991.htm), serving simultaneously as the company's principal executive officer on an interim basis. Stacy J. Smith was elevated to lead independent director.

Werner's background was in solar and semiconductor disruptives rather than in silicon carbide specifically. He had been chief executive of SunPower Corporation from June 2003 to April 2021 — an 18-year run that made him one of the longest-serving CEOs of a publicly traded clean-energy company — and had remained SunPower's chairman through November 2021 before returning as executive chairman in February 2024 as SunPower itself entered financial distress. Earlier, Werner had been chief executive of Silicon Light Machines, an optical MEMS subsidiary of Cypress Semiconductor, and had held senior roles at 3Com. He held undergraduate degrees in industrial engineering (University of Wisconsin) and electrical engineering (Marquette University), and an MBA from George Washington University.

His compensation as Executive Chairman — $150,000 per month in base salary and $225,000 per month in RSUs vesting over one year — reflected the temporary, high-intensity nature of the mandate. Werner stabilised management communications, retained advisers, and shepherded the company toward a restructuring support agreement while the board recruited a permanent chief executive.

## Feurle: The Restructuring Chief Executive

The board [announced](https://investor.wolfspeed.com/news/news-details/2025/Wolfspeed-Inc--Appoints-Semiconductor-Industry-Veteran-Robert-Feurle-as-Chief-Executive-Officer-and-Board-Member/default.aspx) Robert A. Feurle as president, chief executive, and board member on March 27, 2025, with the appointment effective May 1. Feurle, 55 at appointment, brought a career assembled almost entirely inside the European and American semiconductor supply chain. He had begun at Siemens in 1996, moved into Infineon Technologies' early DRAM development organisation in 1999, and spent the subsequent quarter-century in progressively larger executive roles at Qimonda (Infineon's spun-off DRAM subsidiary), Micron Technology, Infineon again, and ams-OSRAM. At ams-OSRAM, he served first as executive vice president and general manager of Image Sensor Solutions from July 2020, then as EVP and GM of the Opto Semiconductors business unit from March 2022 — a unit employing more than 10,000 people globally — until departing for Wolfspeed. He holds an electrical engineering degree from the University of Applied Sciences in Konstanz, Germany, and carries dual US-German citizenship.

One biographical thread carries particular irony. During Feurle's tenure at Infineon from November 2015 to June 2020, the German chipmaker pursued a [proposed acquisition of Wolfspeed's power and RF semiconductor operations](https://www.sec.gov/), a deal announced in 2016 and ultimately blocked by the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States on national security grounds in February 2017. Feurle participated in Infineon's team supporting that bid. Nearly a decade later, he was appointed to lead the company Infineon had tried to buy.

> "Wolfspeed's world-class facilities, exceptional talent, and robust intellectual property position us to maintain and expand our market leadership," Feurle said at appointment.

His compensation reflected the stakes: an annual base salary of $750,000, a performance bonus target of 100 percent of base, a $1 million sign-on bonus payable in two instalments, and an inducement equity package comprising $2.5 million in RSUs and stock options with a Black-Scholes value of at least $2.5 million, followed by an August 2025 regular grant of $2 million in RSUs and $3 million in performance share units tied to relative total shareholder return through July 2028.

## The CFO Carousel and C-Suite Rebuild

Wolfspeed rotated through three chief financial officers inside a single fiscal year. Neill P. Reynolds, executive vice president and CFO, announced his resignation effective May 30, 2025, departing to pursue another professional opportunity. Kevin Speirits, senior vice president of finance who had joined the company in June 2020 and had deep prior experience at NXP Semiconductors and Freescale Semiconductor, stepped in as interim CFO. On July 7, 2025, Wolfspeed announced Gregor van Issum as executive vice president and CFO effective September 1.

Van Issum, 46, arrived from ams-OSRAM, where he had served as executive vice president and group controller and chief transformation and performance officer since June 2020 — making him a direct former colleague of Feurle's. Before ams-OSRAM, van Issum spent eleven years at NXP Semiconductors in finance and strategy roles across multiple business units. He holds a master's degree in information economics from Tilburg University and an executive master's in finance and control from Maastricht. His package: $500,000 base, 75 percent bonus target, $450,000 sign-on, and $3 million in RSU inducement grants.

Rounding out the rebuilt executive team, David T. Emerson, Ph.D., was named executive vice president and chief operating officer effective May 22, 2025. Emerson had spent more than two decades at Cree and Wolfspeed in earlier stints, including as EVP of LED Products, before departing and returning via a consulting role. He holds a doctorate in electrical engineering from Cornell. Melissa Garrett became senior vice president and general counsel, replacing Bradley D. Kohn.

## Board: Demolition and Reconstruction

The board that entered Chapter 11 had been elected at the December 5, 2024 annual meeting and included nine directors. Through the first half of 2025, the roster contracted sharply: Thomas J. Seifert and George H. "Woody" Young III both resigned on April 3, 2025. Mark E. Jensen and Paul V. Walsh, Jr. joined in May 2025 alongside Feurle's board seat — three new directors positioning the board for the restructuring ahead. Jensen, 75, was a retired Deloitte partner who had led the firm's US technology audit practice and simultaneously served on the board of Lattice Semiconductor. Walsh, 61, was the former CFO of Allegro MicroSystems.

The [Restructuring Support Agreement](https://www.sec.gov/), executed June 22, 2025 with holders of more than 97 percent of the senior secured notes, Renesas Electronics America, and holders of more than 67 percent of the convertible notes, set the terms for what would follow. Wolfspeed and Wolfspeed Texas LLC filed voluntary Chapter 11 petitions on June 30, 2025, in the US Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of Texas, Houston Division. The prepackaged plan was confirmed by the court on September 8 and took effect September 29, 2025 — the same date Wolfspeed re-incorporated from North Carolina to Delaware.

On emergence, the five remaining pre-petition independent directors — Thomas Werner, Glenda Dorchak, John Hodge, Darren Jackson, Duy-Loan Le, Marvin Riley, and Stacy Smith — all departed. Five new directors joined:

| Director | Background | Prior Role |
|---|---|---|
| Anthony M. Abate | Chair | COO/CFO Echo360; McKinsey TMT; Air Force radar; Harvard MBA / Duke BS EE |
| Michael W. Bokan | Independent | Retired SVP Worldwide Sales, Micron Technology (29 years) |
| Hong Q. Hou | Independent | President and CEO, Semtech; prior Intel Corporate VP Cloud and Edge; PhD EE, UCSD |
| Eric S. Musser | Independent | President and COO, Corning Inc. (39-year career); West Point; US Army |
| Aris Bolisay | Independent | VP Finance, Renesas Electronics (subject to regulatory clearance at emergence) |

Renesas Electronics America's receipt of approximately 38.7 percent of the new common stock — alongside warrants to purchase 4,943,555 shares at $23.95 exercisable over three years and $203.6 million in new second-lien convertible notes at 2.5 percent due 2031 — made the Japanese chipmaker the dominant shareholder in restructured Wolfspeed. The Bolisay seat formalised that governance anchor. Convertible noteholders collectively received approximately 56.3 percent of new equity alongside new second-lien takeback notes and rights-offering convertible notes.

> "Wolfspeed has emerged from its expedited restructuring process," Feurle said upon the September 29 effective date, "marking the beginning of a new era."

The phrase was precise. The leadership slate entering fiscal 2026 — Feurle, van Issum, Emerson, Garrett, a seven-member board with five seats filled since May 2025 or later — shared almost no personnel with the team that had built and strained the Mohawk Valley project. The institutional knowledge embedded in the fab's process engineers and materials scientists remained; the executives who had designed the capital structure that collapsed did not.

chapters.title: EV Tier-1s, AI hyperscalers, renewable inverters, industrial, merchant SiC wafer customers
chapters.body:
## The Automotive Spine: EV Traction Inverter Design-Ins

For most of Wolfspeed's post-rename existence, the electric vehicle traction inverter represented both the company's clearest commercial thesis and its most visible source of execution risk. Silicon carbide MOSFETs offered a decisive efficiency advantage over silicon IGBTs in 800V EV drivetrains — smaller thermal envelopes, fewer switching losses, higher operating temperatures — and Wolfspeed spent years converting that physics advantage into a stack of automotive design-in commitments.

The most visible of those commitments involved Stellantis.
