The two companies disclosed a multi-year supply agreement for SiC power devices intended for traction inverters across Stellantis's electrified vehicle platforms. Wolfspeed management cited the Stellantis relationship as an anchor customer and one of the clearest validations of the Mohawk Valley 200mm investment thesis. Mercedes-Benz and BMW represented additional disclosed European OEM relationships, consistent with the broader German automaker push toward 800V architectures in premium and performance segments. Volkswagen Group's electrification roadmap similarly placed SiC at the core of next-generation inverter specifications.

Lucid Motors, the California-based luxury EV maker, was among the more explicitly disclosed Wolfspeed device customers. Lucid's Air platform used an 800V architecture from its founding, and the company required high-performance SiC MOSFETs to achieve the range and charging-speed figures that defined its competitive positioning. Wolfspeed's relationship with Lucid illustrated the design-in-to-production pathway: a smaller, technically demanding customer whose platform requirements pushed device performance to the edge of the specification envelope.

The Chinese EV ecosystem presented a structurally more complicated picture. Chinese automakers — including BYD, the dominant domestic EV producer — had initially sourced SiC power devices from Western suppliers including Wolfspeed. But the trajectory through 2023 and 2024 pointed toward accelerating domestication of the SiC supply chain. BYD invested in its own SiC capability, and a cluster of domestic Chinese SiC device makers — supported by government industrial policy — began qualifying parts for Chinese OEM platforms that would previously have been sourced offshore. For Wolfspeed, the Chinese market retained some design-in activity, particularly for higher-specification platforms where domestic SiC supply remained thin, but the long-term displacement risk was structurally elevated.

The broader EV market cycle inflected sharply against Wolfspeed through 2024. Demand forecasts that had underpinned the Mohawk Valley capex case softened materially as Western consumers absorbed sticker-shock on EV prices and adoption curves proved slower than the most optimistic projections. Automotive OEMs pushed out electrification volume timelines, and Tier-1 inverter suppliers reduced near-term SiC device pull. The consequence for Wolfspeed was a painful mismatch: Mohawk Valley was absorbing fixed costs at scale while automotive end-demand provided less volume cover than the ramp model required. Customer design-in commitments remained largely intact — the physics case for SiC in 800V architectures had not changed — but the conversion from design-in to production volume ran behind schedule, and the timing drag became one of the proximate causes of the June 2025 Chapter 11 filing.

## AI Data Centers and the 800V HVDC Inflection

The artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout that reshaped capital-expenditure priorities across the technology industry from 2023 onward opened a new and structurally distinct demand vector for Wolfspeed SiC devices. High-density GPU compute clusters — the GPU server racks built around Nvidia's H100, H200, and Blackwell-series accelerators — operate at power densities that strained conventional 48V power distribution architectures. The response from hyperscalers and rack integrators was a migration toward 800V high-voltage direct-current bus architectures, where SiC MOSFETs provided the switching efficiency and thermal performance required in the AC/DC and DC/DC power-conversion stages.

Wolfspeed's exposure to the Nvidia ecosystem was indirect but strategically significant. Power supply and power-conversion module makers who supplied into Nvidia-based GPU platforms represented a growing segment of Wolfspeed device demand. The 1200V SiC MOSFET was the primary device family relevant to the 800V HVDC application — the voltage headroom required for rectification and PFC stages in a nominal 800V bus system pushed specifications beyond the 650V silicon MOSFET ceiling.

Hyperscaler capital investment in AI infrastructure — Microsoft, Google, Amazon Web Services, Meta, and Oracle collectively committed hundreds of billions in data centre buildout through 2024 and 2025 — created a demand signal that was distinct from the automotive cycle in one critical respect: it was accelerating rather than decelerating in the period when EV demand disappointed. Management noted the AI power-conversion opportunity in earnings commentary as the company sought to demonstrate revenue diversification beyond the automotive concentration that had made 2024 so difficult. The exact revenue contribution of AI power-supply customers was not disclosed with precision in Wolfspeed's segment reporting, but the category was cited as a growth vector in investor presentations through the pre-Chapter 11 period.

## Solar, Wind, and the Renewable Inverter Market

Wolfspeed's solar inverter customer base included SolarEdge Technologies and Enphase Energy, two of the dominant players in the residential and commercial string and microinverter markets. SiC Schottky diodes and SiC MOSFETs delivered efficiency gains in the boost and inversion stages of solar power electronics — a persistent selling point as inverter makers competed on conversion efficiency in a cost-sensitive market.

SolarEdge, however, underwent a severe business contraction beginning in late 2023 and continuing through 2024. A combination of inventory overhang in European residential solar markets, margin compression from Chinese module pricing, and operational missteps produced a collapse in SolarEdge revenues and a significant reduction in its component procurement. For Wolfspeed, SolarEdge's difficulties represented a direct demand headwind: a customer that had been a meaningful SiC device buyer contracted sharply. Enphase showed more resilience, but its microinverter volumes also softened in the US residential solar market as interest rates elevated the cost of rooftop solar financing.

Wind turbine power-conversion represented a more durable if slower-moving segment. Multi-megawatt offshore and onshore wind turbines used SiC devices in the power conversion stages where high switching frequency and thermal tolerance were valued. The customer set was concentrated among a small number of wind turbine OEMs and their Tier-1 power electronics suppliers, and qualification cycles were long. Wolfspeed maintained engagement with this segment as part of its broader renewable energy positioning, though wind contributed less to near-term revenue than automotive or solar.

## Industrial Motor Drives and Rail Traction

Industrial motor drives — used in factory automation, HVAC systems, pumping, and compressor applications — constituted the most granular and geographically distributed segment of Wolfspeed's end-market exposure. The efficiency case for SiC in industrial drives was well established: reduced switching losses at higher frequencies enabled smaller passive components and more compact drive assemblies. The customer set included industrial drive OEMs and the broader white-goods and industrial automation supply chain.

Rail traction represented a smaller but technically demanding application. High-power traction inverters for mainline locomotives, regional electric multiple units, and metro rolling stock operated at the high-voltage, high-current edge of SiC device specifications — a segment where 1700V and 3300V SiC MOSFETs competed with established silicon IGBT platforms that had long track records in a safety-critical environment. European rail electrification programmes and transit system modernisation projects kept this segment active, though qualification timelines limited rapid revenue scaling.

## Merchant SiC Wafers: Supplying the Device Ecosystem

Wolfspeed's merchant SiC substrate and epitaxial wafer business operated across an unusual competitive dynamic: the company's largest device-market competitors were simultaneously among its most important substrate customers. Infineon Technologies, STMicroelectronics, onsemi, Bosch, and Rohm — each of which manufactured SiC power devices in competition with Wolfspeed's own product lines — sourced meaningful volumes of 150mm SiC substrates and epi wafers from Wolfspeed's materials operations.

The arrangement reflected Wolfspeed's structural position atop the SiC value chain. SiC boule growth and wafer slicing required capital, process expertise, and yield management that had taken Wolfspeed decades to accumulate from its Cree Research origins. Competitors had invested in their own substrate capacity — Infineon's Siltectra acquisition brought laser-splitting wafer technology in-house, and Coherent (post-II-VI) built SiC substrate capability — but the industry supply base remained tight enough that external sourcing from Wolfspeed remained commercially rational for device makers who needed wafer volumes beyond what their captive supply could cover.

The 200mm transition complicated the merchant wafer dynamic. Wolfspeed's Mohawk Valley fab and the Saxapahaw materials expansion were designed around 200mm, and the company positioned 200mm substrates as a future merchant supply product as well as a captive device manufacturing platform. For device customers building 200mm SiC fab capacity of their own — or evaluating whether to build it — Wolfspeed's merchant 200mm wafer roadmap was a strategic variable, both as a potential supply source and as a competitive intelligence signal about Wolfspeed's own manufacturing trajectory.

| Merchant Wafer Customer | Primary Relationship | SiC Device Competition |
|---|---|---|
| Infineon Technologies | SiC substrate supply | Direct — CoolSiC MOSFET |
| STMicroelectronics | SiC substrate and epi supply | Direct — SiC MOSFET (Tesla supply chain) |
| onsemi | SiC substrate supply | Direct — EliteSiC MOSFET |
| Bosch | SiC substrate supply | Direct — internal SiC device programme |
| Rohm Semiconductor | SiC substrate supply | Direct — SiC SBD and MOSFET |

The concentration of device-market competitors within the merchant wafer customer list created a persistent strategic tension. Revenue from these relationships provided capacity utilisation and cash contribution during the Mohawk Valley ramp period, but each dollar of SiC substrate delivered to a competitor-customer was a dollar of input supporting devices that competed directly for the same EV, solar, and industrial sockets Wolfspeed was itself pursuing. Management acknowledged this tension as inherent to the vertical SiC business model: wafer supply revenue was additive to the economics, and the alternative — withholding supply to disadvantage competitors — risked antitrust scrutiny and forfeited margin that the company, during its Chapter 11 restructuring period, could not afford to leave on the table.

chapters.title: Where WOLF sits against Infineon, STMicro, onsemi, Rohm, and broader SiC ecosystem
chapters.body:
## A Market With No Pure-Play Peers

The silicon carbide power semiconductor industry arrived at the 2025 restructuring period with an unusual structural characteristic: its only publicly traded pure-play specialist was navigating Chapter 11 while simultaneously operating the world's first dedicated 200mm SiC fab. Wolfspeed occupied a singular position — vertically integrated from crystal boule to finished device, carrying intellectual property accumulated over nearly four decades of SiC materials science, and anchoring US domestic SiC supply-chain ambitions at the moment that ambition became national industrial policy.

Its principal competitors shared none of these vulnerabilities and none of these advantages in identical measure. Infineon Technologies, STMicroelectronics, ON Semiconductor, and Rohm Semiconductor had each scaled meaningfully into SiC through the 2020–2024 EV investment cycle, but all four came from diversified revenue bases that cushioned the blow when that ramp slowed. Each was also, at various points, a Wolfspeed substrate customer — a dynamic that made the competitive map more unusual than a standard peer-versus-peer analysis would suggest.

## Infineon: Cold-Split Wafers and Captive Ambitions

Infineon entered the 2020s as the world's largest automotive semiconductor supplier by revenue, a position built on silicon IGBT and MOSFET dominance across EV traction inverters and industrial power conversion. Its CoolSiC MOSFET and Schottky diode product families grew from a niche position into a scaled business backed by production at its Villach, Austria fab, which Infineon designated as the primary European SiC manufacturing node.

The 2018 acquisition of Dresden-based Siltectra delivered a potential structural cost lever in SiC substrates. Siltectra's cold-split technology uses thermal stress propagation to cleave SiC wafers from boules with reduced kerf loss compared to conventional wire sawing — a meaningful input-cost improvement in an industry where substrate pricing has represented the largest single variable cost for device manufacturers. Whether cold-split would prove commercially decisive at production scale remained a technology execution question as of the frozen window.

Infineon's scale was the primary competitive variable. With annual revenues exceeding €15 billion in fiscal 2024, it could absorb SiC capacity investment without the balance-sheet strain that had proven fatal to Wolfspeed's capital structure. That Infineon had historically been a Wolfspeed substrate customer underscored the supply-chain intimacy at the core of the SiC industry: competitors relied on Wolfspeed materials even as they competed for device sockets downstream.

## STMicroelectronics: The Tesla Effect and the Retrenchment

STMicroelectronics entered the dossier period as the company that had done most to define what SiC commercial scale could look like. Its design-in with Tesla for the Model 3 and Model Y main traction inverter — using STM SiC MOSFETs in the principal power-conversion stage — made it the highest-volume SiC device manufacturer in the automotive segment through the early 2020s. SiC revenue reached an estimated $1.4 billion in 2023, establishing STM as the volume leader in SiC devices ahead of both Wolfspeed and its Japanese peers.

The substrate foundation for that ramp was the 2019 acquisition of Norstel AB, a Swedish SiC substrate specialist, which gave STM a degree of vertical integration comparable to Wolfspeed's — boule growth, wafering, and epitaxy feeding its Catania, Sicily device fab. Catania had undergone multi-year expansion to support the Tesla contract and broader European EV Tier-1 customers.

By 2024, STM was navigating the same demand air pocket that afflicted every SiC supplier: European EV volume projections had been revised sharply downward as automakers extended ICE platform lives and Chinese OEM imports disrupted legacy market share. STM disclosed materially lower SiC revenue guidance for 2025 while reaffirming longer-cycle confidence. The retrenchment removed one source of near-term pricing pressure from Wolfspeed's device-level competitive environment, but confirmed that the EV-dependent SiC thesis was more volatile than the industry's bulls had projected through 2021–2022.

## onsemi: Crystal Growing as Competitive Hedge

ON Semiconductor's approach to SiC vertical integration differed from its peers in one notable respect: it acquired its crystal-growing capability through a transaction rather than organic development. The 2021 acquisition of GT Advanced Technologies — the sapphire and SiC boule grower based in Hudson, New Hampshire — for approximately $415 million gave onsemi control over upstream SiC crystal production and reduced its dependence on merchant substrate suppliers.

onsemi branded its SiC MOSFET product line EliteSiC and established design-in relationships across the EV sector, including announced engagements with Ford Motor Company and Hyundai Motor Group. Its SiC revenue grew substantially through 2022–2023 before encountering the same demand headwinds that compressed the broader market.

The strategic read on onsemi's SiC position was that the GTAT acquisition had partially replicated Wolfspeed's most durable competitive advantage — ownership of the crystal growth process — without the four decades of SiC materials science expertise that Wolfspeed had accumulated since the Cree Research years beginning in 1987.

## Rohm and the Japanese Substrate Ecosystem

Rohm Semiconductor presented a different competitive profile: a Japanese device manufacturer with SiC product lineage extending to the 1990s and a wholly owned European substrate subsidiary, SiCrystal GmbH, headquartered in Nuremberg. SiCrystal gave Rohm a SiC wafer supply position — both captive for its own SCT-series MOSFET and diode production and available to merchant customers — making it one of the few companies globally with vertically integrated SiC operations from crystal to device.

Rohm's design-in wins within the Japanese automotive ecosystem — Toyota, Honda, and their Tier-1 supply networks — positioned it for structural share in a region where domestic sourcing preferences have historically shaped procurement. Resonac (formerly Showa Denko), operating as a SiC substrate merchant supplier without device manufacturing operations, provided a separate source of substrate competition targeting device makers that bought externally. Both companies represented incremental pressure on the merchant wafer revenue line that Wolfspeed carried alongside its device business.

## Coherent and the Substrate Battleground

Coherent Corporation — formed through the 2022 merger of II-VI Incorporated and legacy Coherent — inherited II-VI's SiC substrate operations, based in part in Durham, North Carolina, a few miles from Wolfspeed's research campus. The geographic coincidence underscored how concentrated the SiC substrate industry remained: two of the primary US merchant wafer suppliers were headquartered in the same metropolitan area.

Coherent's SiC wafer business competed directly against Wolfspeed's merchant substrate revenue. In an industry where substrate pricing had been under sustained pressure as 150mm wafer supply expanded through the 2022–2024 period, Wolfspeed's merchant substrate margins faced structural compression from both Coherent on the supply side and a softening device-maker demand picture on the other.

| Company | SiC Model | Key Differentiator | Balance Sheet |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wolfspeed | Pure-play, vertically integrated | First 200mm SiC fab; four-decade crystal IP | Chapter 11 (June 2025) |
| Infineon | Diversified semi + SiC | Siltectra cold-split; Villach scale | Investment-grade |
| STMicroelectronics | Diversified semi + SiC | Tesla design-in; Norstel substrates | Investment-grade |
| onsemi | Diversified semi + SiC | GTAT crystal acquisition; EliteSiC | Investment-grade |
| Rohm | Vertically integrated (Japan) | SiCrystal substrates; Japan OEM base | Japanese listed |
| Coherent | Substrate merchant | II-VI SiC heritage; Durham operations | Post-merger |

## The Chinese Insurgency

The longer-horizon competitive threat to Wolfspeed's substrate business arrived from the Chinese SiC ecosystem. TankeBlue Semiconductor and SICC — both Shandong-based and state-supported — had built SiC substrate capacity primarily at 150mm as of the frozen window, with active programs targeting 200mm wafer diameter. The Chinese government's 14th Five-Year Plan had identified SiC as a strategic semiconductor material, directing both procurement preferences and capital allocation toward domestic supply chains in a manner structurally parallel to the US CHIPS Act framework supporting Wolfspeed's Mohawk Valley investment.

For Wolfspeed's merchant wafer business, the Chinese substitution risk operated on a different timeline than near-term device competition from European and US peers. Chinese substrate quality metrics had improved materially through 2022–2025, and Chinese SiC device manufacturers — including BYD Semiconductor and emerging fabless designers serving domestic EV OEMs — had demonstrated increasing willingness to qualify domestic substrates. The substitution dynamic threatened a portion of Wolfspeed's merchant substrate revenue that had historically flowed to Asian device manufacturers.

## The 200mm Moat and Its Limits

Against this competitive backdrop, Wolfspeed's structural case rested on two propositions. First, the Mohawk Valley 200mm SiC fab represented a genuine technology transition point: 200mm SiC processing yields more die per wafer than 150mm, compresses per-unit substrate costs as utilization rises, and allows use of more mature semiconductor process equipment. As of the frozen window, Wolfspeed remained the only company with a dedicated, high-volume 200mm SiC production fab in commercial operation. Infineon, STM, and onsemi had each disclosed 200mm development programs, but none had matched Mohawk Valley's dedicated production scale or its CHIPS Act–backed US-domestic strategic positioning.

Second, Wolfspeed's crystal growth intellectual property represented institutional knowledge that financial acquisition alone could not replicate. Four decades of SiC boule process optimization — defect density reduction, micropipe elimination, polytype control — had produced process recipes and tooling knowledge embedded in the operational fabric of the materials organization. That competitors had purchased Wolfspeed substrates rather than licensing its crystal technology suggested the IP was more valuable held than monetized as a standalone licence.

The Chapter 11 restructuring cast a shadow over both propositions. Design-in cycles in automotive SiC run three to five years from engineering sample to production volume; customers in that cycle faced the question of whether a supplier navigating bankruptcy proceedings could be relied upon as a sole or preferred source. The pre-packaged restructuring framework — debt-for-equity agreements in place before the June 2025 filing — was designed specifically to minimize operational disruption and preserve customer relationships through emergence. Whether it succeeded in sustaining design-in confidence through the restructuring period remained the operative competitive variable as of May 2026.

chapters.title: Timeline from 1987 Cree founding through 2025 Chapter 11
chapters.body:
## The Compound Semiconductor Pioneer, 1987–2021

Wolfspeed's origins trace to a university laboratory and a material that most of the semiconductor industry had written off as too difficult to manufacture at scale. In 1987, a group of researchers at North Carolina State University founded Cree Research, betting that silicon carbide — a wide-bandgap compound semiconductor capable of operating at voltages, temperatures, and switching frequencies that silicon could not sustain — would eventually underpin the electrification of industry. The founding came six years before the company's 1993 initial public offering on NASDAQ, and the early commercial identity was bound not to power electronics but to light-emitting diodes, where SiC and gallium-nitride substrates enabled the high-brightness blue and white LED revolution of the 1990s and 2000s.

For two decades, Cree scaled its LED franchise into a multibillion-dollar franchise, supplying general illumination, backlighting, and specialty lighting markets. Charles Swoboda, who served as chief executive from 2001 to 2017, presided over the peak of that LED-driven era. But LED commoditisation, driven by intense Asian manufacturing competition, eroded margins steadily through the 2010s, and the strategic logic for retaining a consumer-facing lighting business within a compound semiconductor company weakened with each passing year. Gregg Lowe, who joined as chief executive in 2017 from a senior role at NXP Semiconductors, arrived with a mandate to reposition the company toward power electronics and to pursue vertical integration in SiC manufacturing.

The structural transformation Lowe engineered over his seven-year tenure was the most consequential in the company's history. In April 2021, Cree announced the divestiture of its LED products segment to SMART Global Holdings, which rebranded the unit as CreeLED. The transaction freed the company from a capital-intensive, margin-compressed consumer business and concentrated resources on what management argued was the secular growth opportunity: SiC power semiconductors for electric vehicles, renewable energy inverters, and industrial power conversion. In October 2021, the company completed its renaming to Wolfspeed, Inc. — a signal to investors and customers alike that the Cree identity, associated in the market's mind with LED bulbs, no longer reflected the corporate strategy.

## The RF Divestiture and Pure-Play Identity

One further legacy asset remained. Wolfspeed had retained a silicon carbide and gallium-nitride radio-frequency business serving defence and telecommunications markets under the Cree/Wolfspeed RF brand. In December 2023, Wolfspeed divested that business to MACOM Technology Solutions for $125 million in cash plus $50 million in MACOM stock — a transaction that closed the final chapter of the Cree-era diversification and established Wolfspeed as a pure-play SiC power semiconductor company for the first time. From December 2023 onward, every dollar of revenue, every wafer start, and every capital expenditure dollar was directed at SiC power devices and the substrate supply chain that fed them.

## The Mohawk Valley Wager

The centrepiece of the Wolfspeed transformation was a capital commitment without precedent in the SiC industry. Wolfspeed announced plans to construct the world's first dedicated 200-millimetre SiC wafer fabrication facility in Marcy, New York — the Mohawk Valley Fab — as the cornerstone of a strategy to capture the EV traction inverter market that Lowe publicly described as a once-in-a-generation industrial transition. The facility broke ground in 2022 and achieved initial production operations that year, with a ramp expected to continue through 2024 and into 2026.

The strategic logic was compelling on paper. Moving from 150mm to 200mm SiC wafers would reduce die cost by roughly 40 percent, giving Wolfspeed a manufacturing cost structure capable of serving automotive-grade volume at competitive pricing. The Mohawk Valley site, backed by incentives from New York State and positioned as a beneficiary of the US CHIPS and Science Act's domestic semiconductor manufacturing push, was intended to anchor Wolfspeed's position as the principal US-domiciled SiC supplier at a moment when Washington was actively seeking to reduce dependence on Asian supply chains in advanced semiconductors.

Design-in wins validated the commercial case. Wolfspeed disclosed engagements with Stellantis, Mercedes-Benz, BMW, and the Volkswagen Group across EV traction inverter platforms, alongside Lucid Motors and a broadening base of Chinese EV ecosystem customers. The merchant SiC substrate business supplied Infineon Technologies, STMicroelectronics, onsemi, Bosch, and Rohm — effectively the full roster of SiC device makers that had not built their own SiC boule-growth capability. An emerging AI data-centre opportunity, centred on 800-volt HVDC power-conversion architectures being developed around Nvidia's high-density GPU clusters, added a second growth vector that management began emphasising publicly through 2024.

## Financial Deterioration and the Leadership Succession

The gap between the strategic narrative and the financial reality widened through fiscal years 2023, 2024, and into 2025. Revenue ran in the $750 million to $900 million range, but capacity-utilisation underabsorption at Mohawk Valley — a fab built for volumes that EV market softness and design-in-to-production conversion delays had not yet delivered — generated operating losses that accelerated the consumption of the company's liquidity. The capital structure, heavily burdened by the debt raised to fund the Mohawk Valley buildout, left limited room for operational disappointment.

Gregg Lowe departed as chief executive in November 2024. Thomas Werner, whose prior executive experience included the chief executive role at SunPower, served as interim chief executive during the transition period. In May 2025, Wolfspeed's board appointed Robert Feurle as President and Chief Executive Officer. Feurle brought semiconductor operational experience from Mosaid Technologies and STMicroelectronics, and he assumed the role with the Chapter 11 filing already taking shape in creditor discussions.

## Chapter 11 and the Restructuring Framework

In June 2025, Wolfspeed filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, entering a pre-packaged restructuring framework that had been negotiated with major creditor groups ahead of the filing. The process targeted a debt-for-equity exchange that would substantially reduce the company's funded-debt burden and allow it to emerge from bankruptcy as a going concern with Mohawk Valley operations continuing through the restructuring period.

The forward catalysts that would determine whether the restructuring delivered lasting value were identifiable and specific: confirmation and execution of the Chapter 11 plan of reorganisation; Mohawk Valley utilisation improvement and the yield trajectory at 200mm; conversion of the automotive design-in book into volume production shipments as EV programmes moved from development to launch; scaling of the AI data-centre 800V HVDC SiC opportunity; receipt and deployment of CHIPS Act funding; and the adequacy of the post-emergence capital structure to fund continued operations without the liquidity pressure that had forced the filing.

The path Wolfspeed traced from a North Carolina State laboratory in 1987 to a federal bankruptcy court in 2025 described an arc familiar in deep-technology hardware: a genuinely superior material platform, a capital-intensive manufacturing transition executed ahead of demand, and a balance-sheet reckoning when the demand cycle moved more slowly than the build cycle. The resolution of that reckoning, through the Mohawk Valley ramp and the restructured balance sheet, would define whether the founding bet on silicon carbide had been merely premature or ultimately wrong.

chapters.title: SiC crystal growth IP, 200mm wafer technology, MOSFET design, patent portfolio
chapters.body:
## The Crystal Foundation: Four Decades of SiC Boule Know-How

Wolfspeed's competitive position in silicon carbide derives less from any single patent than from an accumulated body of crystal growth knowledge that began accumulating in a North Carolina State University laboratory in 1987. The company's founders — working from the modified Lely sublimation process and refining the physical vapor transport (PVT) technique — spent the following three decades mastering the conditions under which SiC source material, sublimated at temperatures exceeding 2,000 degrees Celsius, recrystallizes on a seed crystal to form a structurally sound boule.

The engineering challenge is formidable. SiC exists in more than 200 polytypes; the 4H-SiC variant, which delivers the highest combination of electron mobility and breakdown field for power device applications, must be nucleated and grown with crystallographic fidelity across ever-larger boule diameters. Early Cree substrates carried micropipe densities that constrained device yield to levels unacceptable for high-volume power electronics. Over successive decades, the company systematically drove micropipe density toward zero, then turned attention to subtler defects — basal plane dislocations (BPDs) and stacking fault energy characteristics — that remain the frontier of substrate quality improvement and directly determine MOSFET reliability in field operation.

This know-how, accumulated across thousands of growth runs, constitutes what Wolfspeed's annual filings describe as trade secrets that are not fully protected by patents alone. The PVT process involves not just temperature profiles and chamber geometries but empirical mastery of vapor-phase chemistry, seed preparation protocols, and post-growth annealing conditions that take years to replicate even with access to patents describing the general method. When Wolfspeed disclosed the materials expansion at the John W. Pope campus in Saxapahaw, North Carolina, it was building institutional process knowledge into new physical capacity — a transfer that is itself a form of IP generation.

## 200mm: First Dedicated Fab at Mohawk Valley

The transition from 150mm to 200mm SiC wafers represents a structural inflection point for the industry's cost curve. A 200mm wafer carries approximately 78 percent more usable surface area than a 150mm predecessor, enabling significantly more devices per growth run and per lithography pass — a cost multiplication that propagates through every yield-adjusted unit-cost calculation. Wolfspeed moved first. The 538,000-square-foot Mohawk Valley fab in Marcy, New York, constructed with multi-billion-dollar capital expenditure deployed from 2022 through 2025, was designed as a dedicated 200mm SiC manufacturing facility from the ground up — the first such purpose-built 200mm SiC volume fab in the world.

That first-mover position carries an IP dimension beyond the physical plant. Transferring Wolfspeed's device architectures — developed and yield-qualified on 150mm substrates — to 200mm required re-qualification of epitaxial growth uniformity, lithographic overlay accuracy, implant profiles, and gate oxide quality across a larger wafer area and longer thermal gradients. Each qualified process node at 200mm represents a process integration achievement not reproducible from existing public literature, accumulating as proprietary manufacturing IP with each wafer start at Mohawk Valley.

The materials supply chain feeding Mohawk Valley originates at Saxapahaw, where boule growth and substrate slicing capacity was expanded under the capital program the company internally styled the "New Wolfspeed Way." Process continuity running from boule growth at Saxapahaw through substrate preparation, epitaxial deposition, and device fabrication at Mohawk Valley — with research and development anchored at the Research Triangle Park campus — constitutes a vertically integrated IP stack that no single competitor fully replicates at comparable scale.

## MOSFET Architecture and Voltage Classes

Wolfspeed's SiC power device IP spans multiple MOSFET generations and voltage classes. The 650V devices target solar inverters and EV on-board charger applications; the 1200V class dominates EV traction inverter architectures; the 1700V and 3300V devices address industrial motor drives and rail traction converters. The company's C3M planar MOSFET platform addressed gate oxide reliability concerns that had historically constrained SiC MOSFET field adoption — specifically the interface between the gate dielectric and the SiC channel, which is the recombination site responsible for elevated threshold voltage instability distinguishing early SiC MOSFETs from silicon incumbents.

Successive device generations have driven down specific on-resistance (RDS(on)) while preserving or improving switching speed — the figure-of-merit governing the conduction-loss to switching-loss trade-off in a power converter. Each generation incorporates device geometry innovations, implant profile refinements, and contact metallization improvements that attract both patent filings and process trade-secret protection. The breadth of voltage class coverage — from 650V through 3300V — means that Wolfspeed's device IP portfolio spans applications from consumer-adjacent power supplies to heavy industrial power conversion, giving the company licensing and cross-licensing leverage across a wide competitive landscape.

## Patent Portfolio: Scope, Geography, and the Competitive Horizon

Wolfspeed's annual reports disclose a patent portfolio spanning thousands of issued and pending patents, with filings in the United States, Germany, Japan, South Korea, China, and other commercially relevant jurisdictions. The portfolio covers the full SiC value chain: substrate crystal growth, substrate surface preparation, epitaxial layer engineering, device architecture, and packaging. The geographic filing pattern reflects both principal end-market geographies and competitive surveillance of rival SiC programs — particularly in China, where domestic manufacturers including SICC and TankeBlue have grown rapidly behind government industrial policy support.

The SiC IP landscape has become demonstrably more contested. Infineon Technologies acquired Siltectra and its laser-slicing "Cold Split" substrate technology, enabling thinner wafer kerf and higher boule utilization. STMicroelectronics operates its own substrate supply through its Catania boule-growth operations and a Soitec joint venture. Onsemi has pursued substrate self-sufficiency through its acquisition of GTAT's SiC boule-growth program. Rohm holds a substantial multi-decade portfolio anchored in its Tsukuba research operations.

Against this landscape, Wolfspeed's differentiation rests not on patent count alone but on the intersection of issued patents with manufacturing process knowledge that took nearly four decades to accumulate at scale. The US Department of Commerce's CHIPS Act engagement — which identified Wolfspeed's Mohawk Valley facility as strategically significant domestic semiconductor infrastructure — implicitly acknowledged that this process know-how constitutes a national industrial asset, not merely a corporate one. Even through Chapter 11, that accumulated IP stack remained the foundational asset underpinning the debt-for-equity exchange and the creditors' post-emergence equity thesis.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 execution, Mohawk Valley ramp, EV demand cycle, competitive, scale, governance
chapters.body:
## Chapter 11 Execution and Emergence Timing

The most immediate risk Wolfspeed carried into 2026 was the one its own balance sheet created. The June 2025 Chapter 11 filing was structured as a pre-packaged reorganisation, with debt-for-equity exchange agreements already secured from key creditor classes before the petition was filed — a design intended to compress court time and limit operational disruption. Yet pre-packaged does not mean friction-free. Every day the company remained inside the Chapter 11 process was a day customers could invoke force-majeure clauses, a day suppliers could demand cash-in-advance terms, and a day the engineering talent sustaining the Mohawk Valley ramp could evaluate competing offers from Infineon, STMicroelectronics, or onsemi.

The specific emergence timeline — targeting 2025–2026 — carried its own asymmetric danger. A delay of even one or two quarters would extend the period during which automotive Tier-1 procurement teams could accelerate qualification of Wolfspeed-alternative SiC suppliers, compressing the design-in moat that the company spent half a decade and billions of dollars constructing. Creditor coordination risk also persisted: holdout creditors outside the pre-packaged agreement could seek to reopen plan terms, potentially lengthening proceedings at precisely the moment competitors were accelerating wafer capacity expansions of their own. The post-emergence capital structure — materially reduced debt through the equity conversion — was meant to give Wolfspeed the balance-sheet stability to fund continued Mohawk Valley operations, but only if emergence arrived cleanly and on schedule.

## Mohawk Valley Ramp Yield and Utilisation

The second risk was structural and technical: Mohawk Valley could not generate acceptable unit economics until yield rates and capacity utilisation together crossed viable thresholds, and neither variable was moving fast enough to prevent the losses that ultimately forced the Chapter 11 filing.

Wolfspeed had opened the Marcy, New York facility as the first dedicated 200mm SiC fabrication plant in the world — a genuine first-mover achievement. The strategic logic was sound: 200mm wafers carry roughly 1.8 times the die area of 150mm substrates, and the incremental cost per wafer at scale is lower, making the per-unit die cost substantially more competitive once utilisation reaches the mid-double-digit percentages needed to absorb fixed overhead. The problem was the ramp itself. SiC crystal growth and epitaxy are inherently more variable than silicon processes; defect densities — micropipes, threading screw dislocations, basal-plane dislocations — degrade at different rates depending on boule quality, slicing parameters, and epi reactor conditions. Achieving the yield-per-wafer levels necessary to match the device cost-per-amp-hour targets of EV inverter customers required iteration cycles measured in months, not weeks.

Throughout the 2022–2025 deployment period, capacity-utilisation underabsorption was the dominant margin drag, with revenue running in the $750 million to $900 million range against an operating-cost base scaled for higher throughput. The multi-billion-dollar capex committed to Mohawk Valley created a fixed-cost overhang that could only be relieved by throughput growth. A yield excursion — any regression in crystal quality traceable to a feedstock or process parameter shift — could set the ramp back by a quarter or more, resetting the capacity-utilisation trajectory at exactly the wrong moment in the Chapter 11 timeline. Even absent an excursion, the ramp-to-full-utilisation path extended well into 2026 and beyond, leaving a prolonged window during which the gap between revenue and fully-loaded manufacturing cost remained wide.

## EV SiC Design-In Conversion and Demand-Cycle Volatility

Design-in wins are not revenue. This distinction, obvious to any semiconductor veteran, became acutely visible as the EV demand cycle softened materially after 2023. Wolfspeed had assembled a credible automotive customer portfolio — disclosed relationships with Stellantis, Mercedes-Benz, Lucid Motors, and broader Tier-1 traction inverter suppliers, alongside exposure to the European premium-OEM ecosystem — but the conversion from a design-in award to volume SiC shipment requires the end customer's vehicle to reach volume production, which in turn requires consumer demand to sustain the OEM's production schedule.

The EV-cycle volatility of 2024–2025 hit every SiC supplier, but it hit Wolfspeed harder than its vertically integrated peers because Wolfspeed had less diversification across end-markets to buffer the shortfall. European OEMs pushed out EV platform launch dates; Chinese OEMs accelerated, but at price points that squeezed SiC content economics toward domestic Chinese suppliers. The Stellantis relationship, while commercially significant, was exposed to Stellantis's own EV programme revisions. Each such revision represented not just a revenue shortfall but a potential re-qualification event if an OEM redesigned its inverter architecture around a competitor's MOSFET.

The structural uncertainty ran deeper than any single customer relationship. EV penetration trajectories in Europe and North America remained contested by interest-rate effects on vehicle financing, charging-infrastructure gaps, and persistent consumer range anxiety. A slower-than-expected EV adoption curve meant SiC content dollars per vehicle-year would grow more slowly, compressing the addressable volume against which Wolfspeed's Mohawk Valley fixed costs had to be amortised.

## Competitive Intensity

Wolfspeed's competitive map had become crowded in ways that were qualitatively different from the situation at the time of the 2021 renaming. Infineon Technologies, following its acquisition of Siltectra and its internal crystal-growth capability, entered the 2025–2026 period as both Wolfspeed's largest merchant wafer customer and its most formidable device competitor — a structurally awkward dynamic that could resolve in either direction as Infineon's own 200mm SiC wafer capacity scaled. STMicroelectronics had retained the Tesla Model 3 SiC inverter design-in and was executing its own 200mm transition. Onsemi had reoriented its entire SiC commercial strategy around the EV inverter opportunity following its EliteSiC platform build-out.

Beyond Western incumbents, Chinese SiC entrants — including SICC, TankeBlue, and device manufacturers supported by domestic industrial policy — were executing accelerated cost-reduction curves on 150mm and transitioning toward 200mm processes. Their primary vector was price compression in markets where total system cost was the dominant procurement criterion, which described most of the high-volume EV segment in China. For Wolfspeed's merchant wafer business, Chinese substrate suppliers represented a credible and growing threat to volumes from the Asia-Pacific device-maker customer base.

| Competitor | SiC Wafer Capability | Device Focus | Scale Advantage |
|---|---|---|---|
| Infineon | Post-Siltectra internal 200mm in development | Automotive, industrial | Silicon + GaN + SiC portfolio breadth |
| STMicroelectronics | External supply (Wolfspeed, others) + internal | Automotive (Tesla), industrial | Multi-node diversification |
| onsemi | External supply + acquired capacity | EV traction inverter | EliteSiC platform volume ramp |
| Rohm | Internal SiC substrates + devices | Automotive, industrial | Vertically integrated at smaller scale |
| SICC / TankeBlue | Domestic Chinese 150mm/200mm | Chinese EV ecosystem | Policy-supported cost reduction |

## Scale Constraints Against Vertically Integrated Peers

The scale constraint risk was not merely a matter of revenue size. It was structural. Infineon's SiC device business operated as one line inside a company generating roughly $15 billion annually across silicon, GaN, and SiC; STMicroelectronics similarly ran SiC inside a multi-product semiconductor franchise. Both could cross-subsidise SiC ramp costs from mature-node silicon cash flows, weather an EV-cycle softening quarter without existential balance-sheet stress, and offer customers bundled silicon-plus-SiC procurement relationships that a pure-play could not match.

Wolfspeed's pure-play identity, which was its investor-relations positioning rationale, was simultaneously its structural vulnerability. When the EV cycle softened and Mohawk Valley utilisation lagged projections, there were no offsetting silicon or GaN device revenues to cushion losses. The CHIPS Act award — pending disbursement verification against 8-K disclosures — represented one mechanism to partially offset this disadvantage, but grant disbursements are milestone-contingent and cannot substitute for the operating-leverage buffer that vertical integration and portfolio breadth provide to larger peers.

## Governance and Leadership Continuity

The CEO transitions were, by any objective measure, destabilising. Gregg Lowe, who had steered the company from Cree through the LED divestiture and the 2021 Wolfspeed renaming to the Mohawk Valley groundbreaking, departed in November 2024 as financial stress became acute. Thomas Werner served as interim CEO through the pre-Chapter 11 period. Robert Feurle was appointed President and CEO in May 2025, taking the chair during the bankruptcy filing itself — a compressed onboarding window by any standard.

Leadership transitions inside a Chapter 11 process carry compounded risk. The incoming CEO must simultaneously negotiate with creditors, retain customer confidence, manage a complex manufacturing ramp, and establish credibility with a workforce that has watched its equity value approach zero. Feurle brought prior semiconductor executive experience — including roles at Mosaid and STMicroelectronics — but had no established Wolfspeed-customer or Wolfspeed-creditor relationships at the moment he assumed the role. The governance question extending into 2026 was whether post-emergence board composition and the CEO's accumulated institutional knowledge would be sufficient to execute the Mohawk Valley ramp and EV volume conversion at the pace the restructured balance sheet required.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
The twelve months stretching from the frozen snapshot of 23 May 2026 through the corresponding window in May 2027 encompass what amounts to Wolfspeed's first full fiscal year — FY2027, ending the last Sunday of June 2027 — in which the company will operate, or will have recently begun operating, as a restructured entity. The trajectory is more than a financial forecast; it is a test of whether the debt-for-equity exchange that underpinned the June 2025 Chapter 11 filing actually unlocks the operational leverage embedded in the Mohawk Valley 200mm silicon carbide fab ramp.

## The restructuring baseline and the emergence catalyst

By the time of the snapshot, Wolfspeed was expected to have substantially completed the Chapter 11 process or to be in the final stages of emergence. The pre-packaged restructuring framework filed in June 2025 had targeted emergence within the 2025–2026 window, and with creditor agreement in place at the filing date, the administrative timeline was relatively bounded. The first major catalyst of the forward 12-month period is therefore confirmation of the final post-emergence capital structure — specifically the absolute level of remaining debt, the quantum of equity issued to convert creditors, and the terms of any exit financing facility.

That structure dictates everything else. The Mohawk Valley ramp has always represented a viable industrial project at the right cost of capital; the problem through FY2023–FY2025 was that multi-hundred-million-dollar annual interest and refinancing costs sat atop an EBITDA line that was still negative from underabsorption. A cleaned-up balance sheet — combined with CHIPS Act disbursements that have been part of the US-domestic SiC strategic thesis — would alter the unit-economics math materially.

## Quarter-by-quarter catalyst timeline

**Q1 FY2027 (July–September 2026, reported approximately October–November 2026)** is the first clean earnings report under the post-emergence structure. The market will use it as a baseline for post-restructuring operating rates and cash-generation capacity. The Mohawk Valley utilisation rate — which management has consistently cited as the single most important determinant of gross margin — is the primary number to watch. Internal and sell-side models have pointed to a utilisation threshold in the 40–50 per cent range for Wolfspeed to approach breakeven gross margin on a device-level basis; above 60 per cent, the fab economics shift materially. Any Q1 FY2027 disclosure showing Mohawk Valley utilisation trending toward or through the 50 per cent band would reset the consensus narrative.

**Q2 FY2027 (October–December 2026, reported approximately January–February 2027)** captures the seasonally stronger EV and industrial demand periods and, critically, the ramp of automotive EV platforms tied to the Stellantis and Mercedes-Benz design-in wins disclosed during prior cycles. Precise volume-ramp schedules have not been released at the line-item level in public filings, but programme timelines referenced across FY2024 and FY2025 earnings calls pointed to meaningful volume inflection in the 2026–2027 calendar window. Confirmation that design-in wins are converting to production shipments — rather than engineering-sample or low-rate initial-production quantities — is the Q2 threshold event.

**Q3 FY2027 (January–March 2027, reported approximately April–May 2027)** will likely carry the first substantive update on the AI data centre SiC opportunity. The 800V HVDC architecture that Nvidia and hyperscale co-design partners have been specifying for next-generation data centre power delivery creates a structural pull for high-voltage SiC MOSFETs in power-supply stages. Wolfspeed's 1200V device family is the natural candidate. A design-win disclosure or pipeline update tied to a named hyperscaler or Nvidia power-delivery programme in Q3 FY2027 would represent a new leg to the thesis beyond automotive.

**Q4 FY2027 (April–June 2027, reported approximately August 2027)** closes the fiscal year and sets up the FY2028 guidance cycle. The critical unknown is whether CHIPS Act disbursements have been received and deployed at John W. Pope Saxapahaw — the materials expansion site for SiC boule growth and wafer slicing — in a way that materially lowers cost per wafer at Mohawk Valley. Cost-per-wafer improvement is the long-duration driver of the margin story and the basis on which Wolfspeed's structural competitive position against Infineon, STMicroelectronics, and onsemi will ultimately be judged.

## Consensus estimates and implied growth rates

At the snapshot, sell-side coverage — substantially reduced in analyst count following the Chapter 11 filing — had coalesced around a broad revenue range for FY2027 of approximately $760 million to $900 million, implying year-on-year growth of roughly 5–20 per cent from the FY2026 run-rate. The wide band reflects high uncertainty around Mohawk Valley utilisation, EV production schedules at key Tier-1 customers, and the residual effects of the restructuring on customer willingness to commit to new long-term supply agreements.

| Metric | FY2026E | FY2027E | Implied growth |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | ~$730–780M | ~$760–900M | +4% to +19% |
| Gross margin | Negative to ~0% | Low-to-mid single digit % | Inflecting |
| Adjusted EBITDA | Negative | Approaching breakeven | Key threshold |
| GAAP EPS | Deeply negative | Negative, improving | N/M |

GAAP earnings per share remain deeply negative through the forecast period; the relevant operating metric for market participants is adjusted EBITDA or, at the device level, gross margin excluding fab underabsorption charges. A progression from deeply negative gross margin to low-single-digit positive gross margin over the FY2027 period represents the consensus central case. Any miss against this inflection cadence — gross margin still negative in Q2 FY2027, for instance — would likely trigger a substantial re-rating of the post-emergence equity.

## Management guidance and the Feurle frame

Robert Feurle's first full earnings cycle as CEO in the post-emergence period will be watched closely for capital allocation signalling and growth investment posture. In prior quarters, Wolfspeed management framed the Mohawk Valley ramp in terms of the long-cycle EV design-in pipeline, noting that the economic value of the platform was visible even when near-term utilisation was below plan. The question for Feurle's forward guidance is whether he calibrates expectations more narrowly to what Mohawk Valley can demonstrably deliver in FY2027, or whether he re-introduces the longer-arc narrative that has characterised prior management cycles. Given the creditor-appointed board composition expected in the post-emergence structure, guidance discipline and near-term cash management will likely take precedence over expansionary volume commitments.

On CHIPS Act funding, management has noted that programme disbursements are milestone-based and tied to capital spending at the relevant facilities. The forward 12-month period should see at least one update on disbursement receipt, and a confirmed receipt would be a meaningful cash-flow positive event in a period where liquidity management remains closely watched.

## Beat versus miss: the specific thresholds

A **beat** across FY2027 quarters is defined by: Mohawk Valley utilisation disclosed or implied above 50 per cent; gross margin crossing into positive territory on a non-GAAP basis; quarter-over-quarter revenue growth of 5 per cent or more; EV design-in wins transitioning to production-volume language; and CHIPS Act disbursement confirmation.

A **miss** is: utilisation flat or declining from Q4 FY2026 levels; gross margin still negative with no clear inflection schedule in management's forward commentary; any major customer announcing qualification delays or reductions in SiC allocation; CHIPS Act disbursal slippage past calendar year 2026; or evidence that Infineon, STMicroelectronics, or onsemi have captured automotive qualification slots that Wolfspeed was positioned to hold.

## The bull and bear setup

The **bull case** rests on asymmetry: if Mohawk Valley crosses the utilisation inflection point and the post-emergence capital structure has reduced annual interest expense by several hundred million dollars, the incremental contribution margin on each additional wafer is high and fixed costs are predominantly sunk. The net effect is a potential step-change in EBITDA that is non-linear relative to modest revenue growth. Add a confirmed AI data centre design-win and CHIPS Act cash receipt, and the forward 12-month period could establish Wolfspeed as a self-funding industrial growth company rather than a restructuring story. The post-emergence equity, issued at distressed valuations, prices in substantial execution risk — and therefore carries option-like upside if execution is even marginally better than feared.

The **bear case** is that the structural EV demand slowdown — well-documented across 2024–2025 as OEMs and Tier-1 suppliers revised electrification ramp targets downward — has created surplus SiC supply industry-wide, and that Wolfspeed's history of operational misexecution at Mohawk Valley has allowed more disciplined competitors to capture the automotive qualification slots that the 200mm fab was designed to win. In that scenario, utilisation remains range-bound below the breakeven threshold, the balance-sheet benefit of the Chapter 11 exchange is consumed by operating cash burn, and a second recapitalisation becomes necessary before the end of the planning horizon.

The asymmetry at the snapshot favours the bull case in absolute return terms, but the bear case has plausible pathways that are industrial and competitive in nature — not merely financial. That distinction is what makes the next four quarters consequential.

chapters.title: Mohawk Valley ramp, EV/AI scaling, post-emergence capital structure, 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## The Ramp That Rewrites the Economics

When Robert Feurle took the chief executive title in May 2025, he inherited both a restructuring docket and an asset that most of his competitors could not replicate: a 200-millimetre silicon carbide wafer fabrication plant in Marcy, New York, the first of its kind anywhere on the planet. The Mohawk Valley facility had consumed the better part of a decade of capital planning and several billion dollars in construction and tooling expenditure, and by the time Wolfspeed filed for Chapter 11 protection in June 2025, it was still climbing the utilisation curve that separates a money-losing showcase from a commercially viable manufacturing engine. The entire strategic logic of the post-emergence company rested on a single bet: that the world would need far more silicon carbide power semiconductors than the legacy 150-millimetre supply chain could deliver, and that whoever controlled the first scaled 200-millimetre production node would capture the economics that came with it.

The shift from 150mm to 200mm wafers matters for the same reason that any semiconductor node transition matters. A 200mm substrate yields roughly 78 percent more die area than a 150mm substrate, and when the device geometries and process parameters are mature, that translates into lower cost per chip, higher throughput, and the pricing leverage needed to penetrate volume automotive and data-centre platforms. Wolfspeed's management had argued for years that the 200mm transition would be the decisive competitive moat; what they underestimated was the cost of carrying a largely unloaded billion-dollar factory through the trough of an EV adoption slowdown and an automotive supply-chain destocking cycle that stretched from late 2023 through most of 2025. Capacity-utilisation underabsorption became the dominant line item in the company's operating-loss arithmetic, overwhelming gross margin in quarters when Mohawk Valley was running well below its nameplate throughput.

The restructuring framework that emerged from the June 2025 Chapter 11 filing was designed precisely to remove the debt overhang that made carrying those fixed costs existentially threatening. The pre-packaged structure arranged debt-for-equity exchanges with the principal creditor groups, targeting emergence from the court process in 2025 or 2026 with a materially reduced debt load and continuing operations at all manufacturing sites. The Mohawk Valley ramp itself was not interrupted; the legal reorganisation was structured to protect the operational continuity that customers and the US government had an interest in preserving.

## Post-Emergence Capital Structure and CHIPS Act Positioning

The balance sheet that Wolfspeed was expected to carry out of Chapter 11 represented a reset of the capital structure accumulated during the aggressive 2022-2025 fab build-out. With the largest tranche of the legacy convertible and term debt exchanged into equity, the post-emergence entity was projected to carry a leverage ratio that made the fixed-cost burden of Mohawk Valley serviceable against the revenue trajectory that design-in wins implied for the 2026-2028 ramp window.

Equally important to the post-emergence financing picture was the status of the US Department of Commerce CHIPS Act award that Wolfspeed had been pursuing. The company had positioned Mohawk Valley as a flagship example of the domestic SiC supply-chain investment that the 2022 CHIPS and Science Act was designed to incentivise — a domestic, vertically integrated manufacturer of a compound semiconductor deemed strategically critical for electrification and defence applications. The disbursement schedule for any CHIPS Act direct funding, together with the investment tax credit provisions for domestic semiconductor manufacturing, were expected to reduce the net capital cost of the Mohawk Valley build-out and provide a liquidity cushion during the utilisation ramp.

Feurle's initial public posture, consistent with the restructuring communications, was to hold the CHIPS Act negotiations in parallel with the Chapter 11 process rather than allow one to destabilise the other. The Department of Commerce had signalled through the broader CHIPS programme that preserving continuity at US SiC manufacturing sites was consistent with its policy priorities, providing some insulation against the risk that a bankruptcy filing would cause the agency to withdraw or freeze any pending award.

## EV Traction Inverters: Converting Design-Ins to Revenue

The automotive pipeline that Wolfspeed had assembled over the preceding three years — anchoring design-ins with Stellantis, Mercedes-Benz, BMW, and Volkswagen Group platform programmes — represented the volume base on which the Mohawk Valley utilisation thesis depended. SiC MOSFETs in EV traction inverters replace silicon IGBTs and deliver meaningfully higher switching efficiency, enabling longer range from a given battery pack, or a smaller, lighter battery for equivalent range. Those engineering benefits had driven a broad automotive industry consensus that SiC would displace silicon in the main inverter on virtually all premium and high-volume BEV platforms by the end of the decade.

The complication, visible in Wolfspeed's revenue trajectory through fiscal 2024 and 2025, was that automotive design-in wins and production start-of-supply can be separated by three to five years, and the EV demand slowdown in major Western markets compressed the volume ramp on several programmes that had been underwriting the Mohawk Valley loading model. Stellantis, one of the disclosed anchor customers, was simultaneously managing its own production-volume revisions across the Jeep and Ram electrification programmes. Mercedes-Benz had disclosed Wolfspeed SiC content on the EQS platform but was similarly adjusting production cadence.

The 2026-2028 window was expected to see a material inflection as the programmes designed on 200mm-era Wolfspeed devices began volume production. The cost-per-chip improvement from Mohawk Valley — relative to the legacy 150mm Fayetteville baseline — was the mechanism through which automotive customers could reduce inverter bill-of-materials cost enough to make SiC standard-equipment rather than a premium option. Wolfspeed's public positioning was that the 150mm Fayetteville facility would be phased out as Mohawk Valley absorbed its volumes, eliminating a dual-site cost structure and concentrating yield-learning at the advanced node.

## AI Data Centre: The 800V HVDC Adjacency

The emergence of large AI training clusters — anchored by Nvidia GPU racks consuming forty-plus kilowatts per unit — had opened an adjacency opportunity in SiC power semiconductors that was not part of Wolfspeed's original Mohawk Valley business case. High-voltage direct-current power-distribution architectures operating at 800V, adopted by hyperscaler data-centre operators to reduce conduction losses and cable weight across very large rack deployments, created natural insertion points for high-voltage SiC MOSFETs in the power-conversion stages between the utility service entrance and the server rack.

Wolfspeed's 1200V and 1700V SiC MOSFET families were directly applicable to the 800V HVDC bus rectification, power-factor correction, and DC-DC conversion stages where the efficiency premium of SiC over silicon justified the device cost. The customer exposure included both hyperscaler procurement programmes and the power-supply unit manufacturers — server PSU and rack PDU vendors — that supplied directly to the large cloud operators.

The data-centre opportunity was characterised by a faster design cycle than automotive: a power-supply platform re-design could progress from specification to production in eighteen to twenty-four months rather than the forty-eight-plus months typical of automotive traction inverter qualifications. That shorter cycle meant Wolfspeed could address incremental Mohawk Valley capacity with AI data-centre wins on a timeline that partially offset the automotive volume volatility risk.

## Merchant Wafer Supply: The Substrate Leverage

The third revenue pillar — merchant supply of SiC substrates and epitaxial wafers to external device manufacturers — gave Wolfspeed exposure to the entire SiC device ecosystem rather than only its own device design wins. Customers including Infineon Technologies, STMicroelectronics, onsemi, Bosch, and Rohm depended on Wolfspeed substrates as a critical input to their own SiC MOSFET and diode production.

The transition to 200mm substrates in the merchant supply business mirrored the captive device dynamic: customers needed to qualify 200mm material for their own fab processes before they could benefit from the cost reduction, but once that qualification was complete, demand for 200mm wafers would be structurally additive to the 150mm volumes rather than simply substitutive. The Saxapahaw materials expansion — the John W. Pope facility investing in SiC boule growth and wafer-slicing capacity — was the upstream supply-security mechanism for the merchant substrate business, as well as for Mohawk Valley's own wafer input requirements.

## The Feurle Horizon

Feurle's task through the 2026-2030 window was to execute a sequential but overlapping set of transitions: complete the Mohawk Valley ramp from developmental to full commercial utilisation, convert the automotive design-in pipeline into volume revenue that covers the fab's fixed-cost base, establish the AI data-centre channel as a durable second growth leg, and deploy the CHIPS Act funding in a manner that extends US manufacturing leadership in SiC without reopening the capital-structure questions that Chapter 11 had been designed to close.

The company that would execute that agenda was smaller, in financial terms, than the one Gregg Lowe had built — stripped of the LED and RF businesses, reorganised through bankruptcy, and concentrated on a single material system and a single fab as the commercial proving ground. Whether that focus was an asset or a liability depended entirely on whether the SiC cycle delivered the volume inflection that the decade-long Mohawk Valley investment had been sized to serve.

## SiC Value-Chain Portfolio

Wolfspeed's vertical integration spans three layers: **SiC substrates** (150mm in production, 200mm in ramp at Mohawk Valley and materials expansion at John W. Pope facility in Saxapahaw, North Carolina); **SiC epitaxial wafers** (supplied captively and to merchant customers); and **SiC power devices** — MOSFETs rated at 650V, 750V, 1200V, 1700V, and 3300V classes, and Schottky diodes targeting EV traction inverters, AI data-centre 800V HVDC power conversion, solar and wind inverters, industrial motor drives, and rail traction.

## Principal Customers

Automotive (EV traction inverter): Stellantis, Mercedes-Benz, BMW, Volkswagen Group, Lucid Motors, broader Chinese EV ecosystem. Data centre / AI infrastructure: Nvidia 800V HVDC architecture exposure, hyperscaler power-supply chains. Renewable energy: SolarEdge, Enphase Energy, wind power-conversion customers. Merchant wafer: Infineon Technologies, STMicroelectronics, onsemi, Bosch, Rohm.

## Chapter 11 Docket Reference

Filed: June 2025, US Bankruptcy Court. Structure: pre-packaged debt-for-equity exchange with creditor agreement pre-filing. Targeted emergence: 2025–2026. Operational continuity: Mohawk Valley ramp, customer supply agreements, and CHIPS Act engagement continuing through proceedings. Docket accessible via [PACER](https://pacer.uscourts.gov).
